docs.title: Háu! Haŋ! Welcome to Dakhotiyapi.
docs.text:
This course introduces students to the Dakota language using the Standard Dakota Orthography, the writing system developed by Dakota linguists and community educators. Language learning is paired throughout with cultural history from AIS 112: American Indian Studies.

Novice Low → Novice High | 160 days | 8 chapters | 2 semesters

docs.title: About This Course
docs.text:
Dakota (also called Dakhóta, one of the three dialects of the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ / Seven Council Fires) is a Siouan language spoken primarily in Minnesota, North and South Dakota, Nebraska, and Canada. It is closely related to Nakota and Lakota. Dakota was the dominant language of the Great Plains and upper Mississippi before and during European contact, and it remains a living language actively spoken and revitalized by Dakota communities today.

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

  • Greet others using gender-appropriate forms and introduce themselves
  • Count from 1–1,000 and describe things using Dakota descriptors
  • Talk about daily life: activities, body, health, and relationships
  • Engage with Dakota spiritual values and the concept of Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ
  • Describe the land, seasons, and directions in Dakota
  • Connect language to ceremony, oral tradition, and story
  • Understand Dakota treaty history, the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, and contemporary sovereignty

docs.title: Important Notice About This Course
docs.text:
Language Content Under Community Review

The language content in this course — including vocabulary, grammar explanations, example sentences, glossary entries, and interactive games — was generated with AI assistance and has not yet been reviewed or approved by Dakota language speakers or community language authorities.

This content is known to contain dialect inconsistencies and potential inaccuracies, including mixing of Dakota and Lakota forms. It should not be used as a primary language instruction resource until it has been verified by community-approved sources.

This course is currently undergoing review in partnership with Dakota language educators. Language content will be updated to align with materials from Dakhóta Iápi Okhódakičhiye and community-verified sources.

The historical, cultural, and AIS 112 content in this course is based on documented historical record and is suitable for classroom use in the meantime.

We are grateful to our American Indian cultural liaison for identifying these concerns and for guiding the course toward more responsible and accurate materials.

docs.title: A Note on Language and History
docs.text:
Historical Context

The Dakota people were exiled from their Minnesota homeland following the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 — the largest mass execution in American history occurred in Mankato that December when 38 Dakota men were hanged. Thousands more were imprisoned at Fort Snelling or forcibly removed to reservations in South Dakota and Nebraska. Dakota communities have been reclaiming their homeland and language ever since.

Learning Dakota is an act of respect for that survival and resilience. Students are encouraged to approach this language with the same care, humility, and accountability the course material asks of them.

Language as Living Tradition

Dakota is not a historical artifact — it is a living language spoken by communities across the upper Midwest and plains. Many Dakota language immersion programs, master-apprentice partnerships, and community schools are actively working to pass the language to new generations.

Course content follows ACTFL World-Readiness Standards and targets the Novice Low through Novice High proficiency range.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Dakhotiyapi — Beginning Dakota Language is a high school introductory course pairing Dakota language acquisition with AIS 112 American Indian Studies content. Language and history are taught together because they are inseparable — the Dakota language encodes a worldview, and that worldview was the target of deliberate destruction. Learning the language is part of understanding and responding to that history.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
This course follows four commitments:

  1. Language is living. Dakota is not a museum piece — it is actively spoken and revitalized. Learners engage with it as a living tradition, not a historical curiosity.
  2. History is present. The U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, Fort Snelling, the Mankato executions, exile, and boarding schools are not distant events. Their consequences shape Dakota communities today.
  3. Learners have responsibilities. Non-Dakota learners approach this language with humility (wóuŋšila), respect, and honesty about their position as guests in a tradition that was nearly destroyed.
  4. This is a beginning. A year of introductory Dakota opens a door. Students are encouraged to continue, connect with Dakota communities, and support revitalization efforts.

docs.title: Orthography
docs.text: This course uses the Standard Dakota Orthography used by Dakota language programs in Minnesota. The orthography uses accent marks (á, é, í, ó, ú), special characters (č, š, ȟ, ǧ, ŋ), and aspirated consonant notation (čh, ph, th, kh). Regional variations exist and are all valid.

docs.title: Land Acknowledgment
docs.text:
This course was developed on the homeland of the Dakota people — the Bdewákhaŋthuŋwaŋ, Waȟpékhute, Sisíthuŋwaŋ, and Waȟpéthuŋwaŋ peoples. The land was ceded through the 1851 treaties and the aftermath of the 1862 war. Dakota people were exiled from Minnesota but have maintained connections to their homeland and are reclaiming their presence, language, and sovereignty.

Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
• Recall the gender-specific greeting forms (Háu / Haŋ) and their appropriate use
  • List the numbers 1–1,000 in Dakota
  • Name the Seven Council Fires (Očhéthi Šakówiŋ) and their dialect groupings
  • Identify the Standard Dakota Orthography characters and accent marks
  • Recall the four cardinal directions in Dakota
  • Name the seven Dakota values (wačháŋtognaka, ohítika, ksapá, and others)
  • Recognize the Dakota words for seasons, body parts, family relationships, and daily activities
  • List the key events of the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 in sequence

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
• Explain the Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) word order of Dakota and how it differs from English
  • Describe how stative verbs function as color and quality descriptors in Dakota
  • Explain the cultural significance of the tiyóšpaye (extended family band) as the basic social unit
  • Summarize the events of the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, the Fort Snelling imprisonment, and the Mankato executions
  • Explain the concept of Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ (All my relations) and its worldview implications
  • Describe how the passive name construction (emáčiyapi) reflects Dakota values
  • Explain how treaty language affected Dakota land, sovereignty, and community continuity
  • Summarize the role of oral tradition (wóoyake) in Dakota cultural transmission

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
• Introduce themselves in Dakota using name, origin, and formal closing
  • Form future tense (-kte) and negation (-šni) on Dakota verbs correctly
  • Use Dakota vocabulary to describe seasons, land, and directions in context
  • Apply the SOV sentence structure to construct original Dakota sentences
  • Use stative verbs to describe colors and qualities in Dakota
  • Count and perform basic arithmetic communication in Dakota (1–1,000)
  • Apply gender-appropriate speech forms in greeting contexts

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
• Compare Dakota SOV grammar to English SVO word order and explain the cognitive shift required
  • Distinguish between stative verbs and action verbs in Dakota grammar
  • Examine how the 1851 and 1858 treaties reduced Dakota land and examine the legal and cultural consequences
  • Analyze how Dakota vocabulary encodes a relational and land-based worldview
  • Compare Dakota and English name construction and explain what each reveals about cultural values
  • Analyze the role of the boarding school era in disrupting Dakota language transmission

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
• Assess the significance of language revitalization efforts for Dakota communities today
  • Evaluate the impact of U.S. federal Indian policy (boarding schools, Code of Indian Offenses) on Dakota language and culture
  • Judge the role of oral tradition and ceremony in preserving cultural knowledge that was legally suppressed
  • Evaluate the ethical responsibilities of non-Dakota learners engaging with the language

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
• Compose a formal Dakota self-introduction (name, origin, closing) suitable for a community context
  • Write a short paragraph about a season or place using Dakota vocabulary and SOV structure
  • Design a short dialogue between two speakers using greetings, identity phrases, and at least one future tense sentence
  • Produce a cultural reflection connecting a language concept to a historical event or contemporary issue
  • Draft a written response to the question: "Why does Dakota language revitalization matter?"

docs.title: Topics Excluded
docs.text:
This course does NOT cover:

  • Lakota or Nakota dialects (cultural and political context provided, but language instruction focuses on Dakota only)
  • Advanced Dakota grammar beyond Novice High / early Intermediate Low ACTFL level
  • Writing systems other than the Standard Dakota Orthography
  • Ceremonially restricted cultural content
  • Speaking fluency beyond basic communicative phrases at the Intermediate Low threshold
  • Detailed comparative linguistics of the Siouan language family

docs.title: Pronunciation Guide — Standard Dakota Orthography
docs.text: Dakota is written using a Latin-based orthography with accent marks and special characters. The system used in this course is the Standard Dakota Orthography used by the Dakota Language Institute and most Minnesota Dakota communities.

docs.title: Vowels
docs.text:
Dakota has five vowels, each with a short and a stressed (accented) form. Accent marks indicate both stress and a slightly different quality.

Written Sounds Like Example English a a in "father" ata his/her body á a in "father" (stressed, longer) máza metal / iron e e in "café" eya he/she said i ee in "see" inila quiet í ee in "see" (stressed) wíčhaša man o o in "go" oŋ to use ú oo in "moon" (stressed) ú to come

Accent Marks = Stress

In Dakota, the accent mark (á, é, í, ó, ú) marks the stressed syllable. Unlike English, where stress is unpredictable, learning Dakota accent placement will significantly improve your pronunciation.

docs.title: Consonants — Special Characters
docs.text:
Most Dakota consonants are similar to English. The following require attention:

Written Sounds Like Example English č ch in "church" čhaŋté heart š sh in "shoe" šúŋka dog ȟ ch in German "Bach" (back of throat) ȟaŋhépi night ǧ voiced version of ȟ (gargled) waǧáčhaŋ cottonwood ŋ ng in "sing" waŋží one ź zh like s in "measure" — (rare) ' (glottal stop) brief throat catch, like "uh-oh" ič'íčaǧa to make for oneself

docs.title: Aspirated Consonants
docs.text:
Dakota distinguishes plain, aspirated, and ejective consonants — a three-way distinction English does not have:

Type Written Example Explanation Plain p, t, k, č tópa (four) like English p/t/k Aspirated ph, th, kh, čh čhaŋté (heart) with a strong puff of air Ejective p', t', k', č' — sharp, popping sound

Aspirated Consonants Are Common

In Dakota, the aspirated forms (ph, th, kh, čh) appear frequently. The h after the consonant is NOT a separate sound — it marks aspiration. So čhaŋté (heart) is one syllable cluster: "chh-aŋ-tay."

docs.title: Gender Differences in Speech
docs.text:
Dakota has one of the most well-known gender distinctions in Indigenous North American languages: men and women use different words for greetings and some sentence-final particles.

Expression Male Form Female Form Hello / greeting Háu Haŋ Yes Háŋ Háŋ (same) Sentence-final affirmation -ye or -yelo (male) -ye (female, softer)

Why Gender Distinctions in Language?

The male/female speech distinction in Dakota reflects traditional social roles and speech contexts. Today, many Dakota speakers use both forms fluidly, especially in mixed-gender settings. The distinction is not rigid in contemporary use but is important to understand historically and in formal or ceremonial contexts.

docs.title: Nasalized Vowels
docs.text:
The character ŋ after a vowel nasalizes it (adds an ng resonance through the nose). This changes the sound and the meaning:

  • waŋ = a (article/particle) vs. wa = snow
  • oŋ = to use vs. o = to hit/shoot (in some forms)

docs.title: Dakota Grammar — Key Features
docs.text:
SOV Word Order

Dakota is a Subject-Object-Verb language — the verb comes at the end. "I eat bread" becomes "I bread eat" in Dakota structure. This is one of the biggest adjustments for English speakers.

Future Tense with -kte

The future tense in Dakota uses the suffix -kte at the end of the verb: mduté (I eat) → mduté kte (I will eat). This contrasts with Ojibwe, which uses a prefix (inga-).

Stative Verbs

Many Dakota "adjectives" are actually stative verbs — they describe a state of being. "The dog is black" uses a verb meaning "to be black," not an adjective modifying a noun.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Chapter 1 introduces Dakota greetings, introductions, and identity. Students encounter one of Dakota's most distinctive features immediately: men say Háu to greet, women say Haŋ. Identity in Dakota is rooted in the tiyóšpaye — the extended family band — and in one's relationship to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ (Seven Council Fires). AIS 112 content covers the pre-contact political structure of the Dakota nation.

docs.title: AIS 112 Cultural Context — Weeks 1–4
docs.text:
The Očhéthi Šakówiŋ — Seven Council Fires

Long before European contact, the Dakota people were organized into the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ — the Seven Council Fires. These were not separate tribes but seven related peoples sharing a common language family and political structure. The Dakota (four eastern fires) lived primarily in Minnesota's lakes and forests; the Nakota (middle fires) lived on the eastern plains; the Lakota (western fire) lived on the northern Great Plains.

Decision-making was communal and consensus-based. Leadership was earned through demonstrated wisdom, bravery, and generosity — not inherited. The akíčhita (soldier societies) helped maintain community order.

Tiyóšpaye

The tiyóšpaye (extended family band) was the basic unit of Dakota society — a group of related families who camped, hunted, and governed together. Identity began with your tiyóšpaye, not with the individual. A Dakota person introduced themselves by naming their tiyóšpaye and their place within it.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The first thing Dakota students notice is that greetings have a gender distinction: men say Háu, women say Haŋ. This is not about hierarchy — it is about clarity and tradition in a language that encodes social relationships deeply. Both forms mean essentially the same thing: a warm acknowledgment of the person in front of you.

The concept closest to Dakota identity is the tiyóšpaye — your extended family group. Before you share your name in traditional Dakota, you share your people. Who you are is inseparable from who raised you, who you belong to, and who you are responsible for.

"it's not different" Léčhaŋna LEH-chahn-nah See you soon

Grammar: Gender Speech in Dakota

The male/female speech distinction (Háu vs. Haŋ) is one of the most famous features of Dakota and Lakota. It extends beyond greetings to sentence-final particles: males may add -yelo or -lo to statements; females use -ye or softer endings. In this course, both forms are taught so students understand and recognize them in context.

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: Pidámayaye
docs.text:
Word Breakdown: Pidámayaye — "thank you" Part Form Meaning ROOT pidá- to be pleased / glad PREFIX -ma- me (first person object) SUFFIX -yaye you cause / you make

Analysis: "Thank you" in Dakota literally means "you cause me to be glad / you make me pleased." Gratitude is expressed as an action the giver performs on the receiver — a fundamentally relational framing. Compare with Ojibwe miigwech, which is rooted in the concept of giving.

docs.title: Example Conversation 1
docs.text: Dakota English A (male): Háu! Hello! B (female): Haŋ! Pidámayaye bi-yápi. Hello! Thank you for coming. A: Háŋ, pidámayaye. Yes, thank you. B: Tokhéya. Goodbye.

docs.title: Introduction Vocabulary
docs.text:
Dakota English Notes Táku eníčiyapi he? What is your name? Lit. "What do they call you?" ___ emáčiyapi My name is ___ Lit. "They call me ___" Tókheya yaúŋ he? Where are you from? ___ etáŋhaŋ waúŋ I am from ___ Mitiyóšpaye My tiyóšpaye / my family band Očhéthi Šakówiŋ Seven Council Fires the Dakota nation

Grammar: Names as Passive Constructions

Dakota names work differently from English. Instead of "My name IS ," Dakota says "They CALL ME " — emáčiyapi. This passive construction reflects how identity in Dakota is socially conferred, not self-declared. You are named by your community.

  • emáčiyapi = they call me (what my name is)
  • eníčiyapi = they call you (what your name is)
  • ečhíyapi = they call him/her

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: Emáčiyapi
docs.text:
Word Breakdown: emáčiyapi — "they call me / my name is" Part Form Meaning ROOT e- to say / to call INFIX -má- me (first person object) INFIX -či- you (second person — in some forms this is absorbed) SUFFIX -yapi they (third person plural actor)

Full meaning: "They [the people] call me [by this name]." Identity is socially bestowed — your name exists because others give it to you and call you by it.

Dakota English Bdewákhaŋthuŋwaŋ Mdewakanton — "Spirit Lake Village" Waȟpékhute Wahpekute — "Shooters among the Leaves" Sisíthuŋwaŋ Sisseton — "Village of the Swamp" Waȟpéthuŋwaŋ Wahpeton — "Village in the Leaves" Tiyóšpaye extended family band Oyáte nation / people Akíčhita soldier / warrior society Wičhášta man (wíčhaša in some dialects) Wiŋyaŋ woman

AIS 112 Connection — Pre-Contact Political Structure

The Dakota operated without a centralized government or hereditary chieftainship in the European sense. Leadership was fluid and earned: a man or woman demonstrated leadership through generosity (wačháŋtognaka), bravery (ohítika), and wisdom (ksapá). The Council of Seven Fires coordinated through annual gatherings and through shared cultural identity rather than through a bureaucratic chain of command.

This decentralized, consensus-based political structure was systematically misunderstood by U.S. treaty negotiators, who often signed agreements with individual leaders who did not have the authority to cede land on behalf of the entire people.

B: Tókheya yaúŋ he? Where are you from? A: Bdewákhaŋthuŋwaŋ etáŋhaŋ waúŋ. I am from Mdewakanton. B: Pidámayaye! Tokhéya. Thank you! Goodbye.

Sample: | Dakota | English | |--------|---------| | A (m): Háu! Táku eníčiyapi he? | Hello! What is your name? | | B (f): Haŋ! Maria emáčiyapi. Gíčhi? | Hello! My name is Maria. And you? | | A: James emáčiyapi. Pidámayaye. | My name is James. Thank you. | | B: Tokhéya! | Goodbye! |

15. Explain the gender speech distinction in Dakota. What forms does it take, and what does this tell us about the role of social categories in the language? (4–6 sentences)

Answer 15

Strong answers: men say Háu, women say Haŋ; extends to sentence-final particles (male -yelo/-lo, female -ye); not a hierarchy but a social distinction encoded in grammar; reflects traditional roles and speech contexts; contemporary speakers may use both forms fluidly; important for learners to recognize both.

16. Describe the pre-contact Dakota political structure. What is the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ? How was leadership organized? Why did U.S. treaty negotiators misunderstand this system? (4–6 sentences)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Chapter 2 introduces the Dakota number system from one to ten, a set of color terms that function as stative verbs rather than adjectives, and descriptive vocabulary for everyday objects. Students learn one of Dakota's most fundamental grammatical distinctions: in Dakota, words like "red" or "white" are not adjectives modifying a noun — they are stative verbs describing a state of being. AIS 112 content introduces the Oceti Sakowin's relationship with the land and how colors held sacred significance in Dakota ceremony.

docs.title: AIS 112 Cultural Context — Weeks 3–5
docs.text:
Colors in Dakota Ceremony and Worldview

In Dakota spiritual practice, the four cardinal directions are associated with specific colors that carry meaning far beyond aesthetics. Red (šá) is associated with the east and new beginnings. Black (sápa) is associated with the west and transformation. White (sáŋ) is associated with the north and purity. Yellow-gold (žiží) is associated with the south and growth. These associations appear in ceremony, regalia, and in the decoration of sacred objects. When you learn Dakota color words, you are also learning a layer of cosmological meaning.

Dakota Counting and Trade

Before European contact, the Dakota peoples used a decimal counting system that enabled trade, measurement of time, and the counting of horses, bison, and winter counts. The waniyetu wowapi (winter count) was a pictographic calendar kept on bison hide; keepers of these counts tracked years by significant events. Numbers were essential to this practice. The Dakota decimal system — base 10 — mirrors the structure of many world languages and suggests a long tradition of quantitative thinking.

Stative Verbs vs. Adjectives

A common error for English speakers is to treat Dakota color words as adjectives that come before a noun ("the red horse"). In Dakota, color words are stative verbs — they describe a condition or state. The correct structure places the color word after the noun: šúŋka kiŋ šá = "the dog, it-is-red" (the red dog). This verb-like behavior is consistent with how Dakota grammar treats most descriptive states.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Chapter 1 — Háu / Haŋ: Greetings & Identity — Complete before beginning Chapter 2. Students should be comfortable with Dakota pronunciation, accent marks, and the concept of gendered greetings.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
When English speakers learn a new language, they often expect to find adjectives that work just like English ones — words placed before a noun that describe it. Dakota surprises students here. There are no adjectives in the traditional English sense. Instead, Dakota uses stative verbs — verb forms that describe a state of being — to express what English calls descriptive qualities. "Red" is not a property a horse has; it is a state the horse is in.

This grammatical distinction is not a quirk. It reflects something deeper about how Dakota organizes the world: states, conditions, and qualities are dynamic, not fixed. A thing can be red the way a fire can be burning. This philosophy of ongoing relationship between objects and their qualities is woven through the language.

Numbers in Dakota follow a similar logic of relationship and combination. Once you know the numbers one through ten, you can construct all numbers up to one hundred through a transparent, logical system of combination. The word for eleven is literally "ten and one more." The elegance of this system made it practical for trade, ceremony, and the keeping of records across generations.

"one bent back" (nine fingers) wikčémna wik-CHEHM-nah ten

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: napčíyuŋka
docs.text:
Break down the word for "nine" Morpheme Meaning napč- from nápe (hand) -í- directional/reflexive infix -yuŋka to lie/bend back

Analysis: The word for nine encodes a body-based counting gesture — nine fingers with one "bent back" or held down. This is a trace of a tactile, embodied counting system where the body itself was the original counting tool. Many indigenous number systems show similar somatic origins. When students learn napčíyuŋka, they are preserving memory of how Dakota people first counted — with their hands.

docs.title: Numbers 11–20: Compound Formation
docs.text:
Dakota English Structure wikčémna waŋží aké waŋží eleven ten + one + more/again + one wikčémna waŋží aké núŋpa twelve ten + one + more + two wikčémna waŋží aké yámni thirteen ten + one + more + three wikčémna waŋží aké tópa fourteen ten + one + more + four wikčémna waŋží aké záptaŋ fifteen ten + one + more + five wikčémna núŋpa twenty ten × two wikčémna yámni thirty ten × three

Grammar: The Compound Number Pattern

Numbers above ten are formed transparently: wikčémna (ten) + the tens multiplier + aké (again/more) + the ones digit. This additive, transparent structure means you never need to memorize arbitrary forms — you build them from parts you already know.

docs.title: Example Sentences: Counting
docs.text: Dakota English Šúŋka núŋpa yuhápi. They have two dogs. Tóna yukhéha he? How many do you have? Waŋží héčhiŋyaŋ. Just one. Wikčémna waŋží čhaŋpá yuhápi. They have ten horses. Záptaŋ wičhášta kiŋ hí. Five men came.

docs.title: Section 2 — Colors as Stative Verbs
docs.text:
Grammar: Stative Verbs for Color

In Dakota, color words function as intransitive stative verbs. This means they conjugate for person and can appear as predicates. The basic construction is:

[Noun] + kiŋ + [color-verb]

  • Šúŋka kiŋ šá. = The dog is red.
  • Wówapi kiŋ tó. = The book is blue/green.

To make a color word modify a noun in an English adjective-like way, Dakota uses a relative clause structure or a nominalizer suffix.

docs.title: Key Vocabulary: Colors
docs.text: Dakota Pronunciation English Notes šá SHAH red Also: crimson, scarlet; sacred in ceremony tó TOH blue / green One word covers both blue and green ğí GHEE brown / tan / yellow Earth tones; also describes tawny animals sáŋ SAHN white / whitish Off-white, cream; winter associations sápa SAH-pah black Night, the west, transformation žiží ZHEE-zhee yellow-orange Golden; sun, south, growth lúta LOO-tah bright red More intense than šá; sometimes ceremonial

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: sápa
docs.text:
Break down the word for "black" Morpheme Meaning sá- a root suggesting brightness/contrast -pa a suffix indicating completeness or depth

Analysis: The word sápa for black is interesting because it shares a root with sáŋ (white/whitish) — both seem to involve a base related to perceptual contrast. This root pattern suggests that the Dakota color system may have originally organized colors around degrees of light/darkness before expanding into hue distinctions. The pairing of sáŋ and sápa mirrors the pairing of north and west in ceremonial direction symbolism.

docs.title: Color Conjugation: First and Second Person
docs.text:
Stative verbs conjugate by inserting a personal prefix. For color verbs, the first-person prefix is ma- and the second-person prefix is ni-:

Person Dakota English I am (red) mašá I am red (describing my state/blush) You are (red) ništá You are red He/She/It is (red) šá (it) is red — no prefix I am (black) masápa I am black (I am wearing black/in darkness) You are (black) nisápa You are black

docs.title: Example Sentences: Colors
docs.text: Dakota English Čhaŋpá kiŋ žiží. The horse is golden/yellow. Maȟpíya kiŋ tó. The sky is blue. Makȟá kiŋ ğí. The earth is brown. Wápa kiŋ sáŋ. The snow is white. Háŋpa kiŋ sápa. The moccasin is black. Čhaŋpá šá čhiŋ hí. The red horse came.

docs.title: Key Vocabulary: Basic Descriptors
docs.text:
Dakota Pronunciation English Notes čísčila CHEES-chee-lah small, little Diminutive -la adds softness tháŋka THAHN-kah big, large téča TEH-chah new kȟáŋta KHAHN-tah old (of objects) Do not use for people waŋká WAHN-kah old (of people) Respectful; use only for elders čhaŋtéčhila chahn-TEH-chee-lah beloved, dear Lit. "heart-small" = treasured téča šni TEH-chah SHNEE not new, old Negation with šni tȟáŋka šni THAHN-kah SHNEE not big, small

AIS 112 Connection: Diminutives and Kinship

The diminutive suffix -la / -na appears throughout Dakota in terms of endearment and kinship. Čhuwítkala (younger sister, female speaking) contains -kala as a diminutive of čhuwítka. This suffix signals smallness but also tenderness — the small one who is beloved. Understanding diminutives is essential for reading Dakota kinship terms in Chapter 4.

Chapter 2 Quiz

docs.title: Chapter 2 Quiz — Otóiyohi: Numbers, Colors & Descriptors
Part A — Multiple Choice (10 questions, 2 points each)
docs.text:
1. What is the Dakota word for the number seven? Answer

b) šakówiŋ

šakówiŋ is the Dakota word for seven. záptaŋ = five, šákpe = six, šaglóğaŋ = eight.

a) záptaŋ b) šakówiŋ c) šákpe d) šaglóğaŋ

2. In Dakota grammar, color words like šá (red) function as: Answer

c) Stative verbs

Color words in Dakota are stative verbs that describe a state of being. They conjugate for person and number and act as predicates, not modifiers placed before a noun as English adjectives do.

a) Adjectives placed before the noun b) Adjectives placed after the noun c) Stative verbs d) Adverbs

3. Which color term covers BOTH blue and green in Dakota? Answer

a) tó

tó covers the blue-green spectrum in Dakota. There is no separate word distinguishing blue from green in traditional Dakota; the single term tó covers sky, water, and foliage alike.

a) tó b) šá c) ğí d) žiží

4. What does wikčémna mean? Answer

b) ten

wikčémna = ten. It is the base unit for building larger numbers: wikčémna núŋpa = twenty, wikčémna yámni = thirty, etc.

a) one hundred b) ten c) twenty d) five

5. How is the number eleven expressed in Dakota? Answer

c) wikčémna waŋží aké waŋží

The compound number eleven = wikčémna (ten) + waŋží (one) + aké (again/more) + waŋží (one). The word aké signals "and one more added."

a) wikčémna tópa b) waŋží wikčémna c) wikčémna waŋží aké waŋží d) núŋpa wikčémna

6. Which Dakota sentence correctly expresses 'The horse is golden/yellow-orange'? Answer

b) Čhaŋpá kiŋ žiží.

The correct pattern is [noun] + kiŋ (the definite article/focus particle) + [color-stative-verb]. čhaŋpá = horse, kiŋ = the, žiží = yellow-orange.

a) Žiží čhaŋpá kiŋ. b) Čhaŋpá kiŋ žiží. c) Kiŋ čhaŋpá žiží. d) Čhaŋpá žiží kiŋ.

7. What does the word napčíyuŋka (nine) literally encode? Answer

a) A body-based counting gesture — nine fingers with one bent back

The word napčíyuŋka derives from nápe (hand) and yuŋka (to lie/bend). It encodes the gesture of holding down one finger, leaving nine extended — a tactile, embodied counting method.

a) A body-based counting gesture — nine fingers with one bent back b) The number of months in a winter count c) The count of original council fires d) The number of clan groups

8. The Dakota word sápa means: Answer

c) black

sápa = black. It shares a root with sáŋ (white/whitish), suggesting an original contrast-based color classification. sápa is associated with the west and transformation in Dakota ceremony.

a) white b) brown c) black d) blue

9. Which Dakota word should you use to describe an elder person as 'old'? Answer

b) waŋká

waŋká is used respectfully for elders (people). kȟáŋta means old for objects. Using the wrong term would be disrespectful — a key cultural distinction embedded in the language.

a) kȟáŋta b) waŋká c) téča d) čísčila

10. In Dakota ceremony, what direction is associated with the color red (šá)? Answer

a) East

Red (šá) is associated with the east and new beginnings in Dakota ceremonial tradition. The four directions each carry a color: east/red, west/black, north/white, south/yellow-gold.

a) East b) West c) North d) South

docs.title: Part B — Fill in the Blank (3 questions, 5 points each)
docs.text:
11. Complete the Dakota sentence for 'The sky is blue': Maȟpíya ____ tó. Answer

kiŋ

Maȟpíya kiŋ tó. — The definite article/focus particle kiŋ links the subject noun to the stative verb predicate. The full sentence: Maȟpíya kiŋ tó. = "The sky is blue/green."

12. Write the Dakota words for the numbers three, six, and nine. Answer
  • Three: yámni
  • Six: šákpe
  • Nine: napčíyuŋka

These three numbers are commonly confused. Memory tip: yámni (3) rhymes with "mommy"; šákpe (6) starts with the same šak- as šakówiŋ (7); napčíyuŋka (9) is the long "finger" word.

13. The diminutive suffix in Dakota that expresses smallness and tenderness, seen in words like čhuwítkala, is: ____ Answer

-la (also appears as -na)

The suffix -la / -na expresses diminutive size and emotional tenderness. It appears in kinship terms, terms of endearment, and in words like čísčila (small). Understanding this suffix is essential preparation for Chapter 4 kinship vocabulary.

docs.title: Part C — Short Answer (3 questions, 10 points each)
docs.text:
14. Explain in your own words why Dakota color words are grammatically different from English adjectives. Give one example sentence in Dakota with an English translation that demonstrates this difference. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student clearly explains that Dakota color words are stative verbs (not adjectives), that they describe a state of being rather than modify a noun, and that they appear after the noun in predicate position rather than before it. Student provides a grammatically correct example sentence such as Šúŋka kiŋ šá. (The dog is red.) with correct translation.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student understands the concept but explanation is incomplete, or example sentence has a minor error.

Sample answer: "In English, 'red' is an adjective placed before the noun: 'the red dog.' In Dakota, šá (red) is a stative verb — it describes a state the dog is in, not a property it has. The correct Dakota sentence is Šúŋka kiŋ šá, which literally means 'the dog, it-is-red.' The color word comes after the noun and acts as the predicate of the sentence."

15. What is a waniyetu wowapi (winter count) and how did the Dakota number system support this practice? Connect your answer to at least one specific number term from this chapter. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student correctly identifies waniyetu wowapi as a pictographic year-count kept on bison hide, explains that each year was recorded by a significant event, and connects this to the decimal number system. Student references at least one specific number term accurately.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student identifies the winter count correctly but makes only a general connection to numbers without citing a specific term, or vice versa.

Sample answer: "A waniyetu wowapi is a pictographic calendar — a record of years kept on bison hide by designated keepers in a Dakota community. Each year was marked by a single significant event: a great battle, an unusual winter, a celestial event. The Dakota decimal number system (base 10, using wikčémna for ten as the core unit) made it possible to count and communicate the passage of years precisely. For example, saying wikčémna yámni (thirty years) clearly expressed how many winters had passed since a certain event, helping communities maintain accurate oral and pictographic records across generations."

16. Describe the ceremonial significance of at least two Dakota color terms. How does understanding these meanings change how you read the Dakota color vocabulary as a whole? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately describes the ceremonial/directional associations of at least two colors (e.g., red/šá = east/new beginnings; black/sápa = west/transformation; white/sáŋ = north/purity; yellow-gold/žiží = south/growth). Student reflects on how this context transforms color vocabulary from simple description to cosmological meaning.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student identifies ceremonial significance of two colors but does not reflect on the broader implications for language learning.

Sample answer: "Red (šá) is associated with the east and new beginnings — the direction of sunrise, of birth, of starting. Black (sápa) is associated with the west and transformation — the direction of sunset, of endings that are also transitions. Knowing this changes how I read the color vocabulary. These aren't just words for labeling objects; they are carriers of a whole cosmological framework. When a Dakota speaker says a robe is šá, they may be expressing not just its color but its sacred orientation — that it belongs to the energies of the east. The language encodes the worldview."

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Wóuŋsipi: Daily Life & Action Verbs
Summary
docs.text: Chapter 3 introduces the Dakota action verb system, daily-life vocabulary, and the language's fundamental SOV (Subject-Object-Verb) word order. Students learn how to conjugate active verbs in the present and future tenses, using the future suffix -kte and the negation suffix -šni. AIS 112 content covers the structure of traditional Dakota daily life — the rhythms of the tiyóšpaye across seasons — and how language reflected communal responsibility over individual action.

docs.title: AIS 112 Cultural Context — Weeks 5–7
docs.text:
Daily Life in the Tiyóšpaye

Traditional Dakota daily life was organized around the tiyóšpaye — the extended family band. Responsibilities were distributed by age, gender, and clan role, not by individual preference. Women managed the tipi, processed food, and maintained the camp; men hunted, engaged in diplomacy, and protected the community. Children learned by doing, watching elders, and participating from an early age. There was no sharp separation between "work" and "life" — tending horses, preparing food, telling stories, and praying were all part of a continuous daily practice.

Language and Collective Action

Dakota verbs encode collective action grammatically. The inclusive first-person plural (uŋ-...-pi, "we including you") and exclusive (uŋ-...-pi vs. other forms) distinguish whether the listener is part of the group acting. This is not a minor detail — it is a grammatical expression of the Dakota value of wóčhekiye (prayer/relatedness): when you say "we," Dakota grammar asks you to specify whether you mean "we with you" or "we without you." English collapses this distinction; Dakota preserves it.

SOV Word Order

English word order is SVO: Subject → Verb → Object ("The woman eats the berry"). Dakota word order is SOV: Subject → Object → Verb ("The woman the-berry eats"). This is one of the most important structural differences to internalize. Do not translate word-by-word from English — restructure the sentence entirely.

docs.text: Chapter 1 — Háu / Haŋ and Chapter 2 — Otóiyohi. Students should be familiar with Dakota pronunciation, basic noun vocabulary, and the concept of stative verbs.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Every language has a "skeleton" — a basic sentence structure that everything else hangs from. In English, that skeleton is Subject-Verb-Object: The hunter sees the deer. In Dakota, the skeleton is Subject-Object-Verb: The hunter the-deer sees. This single difference restructures everything about how you build a sentence. The verb — the action, the heart of what's happening — comes at the end, like a conclusion.

This is not arbitrary. Linguists have observed that SOV languages tend to cluster with certain other features: postpositions rather than prepositions, relative clauses before nouns rather than after them, adjectives (or stative verbs) after nouns rather than before. Dakota is consistent in this way: the language is built so that context accumulates and the core meaning lands last.

Learning to think in SOV order requires unlearning English habits. The exercises in this chapter ask you to build sentences from the ground up, placing the verb last every time — not as a rule to memorize, but as a way of thinking.

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: wayáwa
docs.text:
Break down the verb "to read / to count" Morpheme Meaning wa- general object prefix (indefinite direct object) -yáwa to count, to reckon

Analysis: wayáwa originally meant "to count" — to reckon numbers. With the arrival of written language and formal schooling, the word expanded to cover reading as well, since reading involves the same act of reckoning symbols. This semantic expansion tells a history: it marks the moment Dakota communities encountered written text as a counting-like cognitive act. The word wayáwa also appears in the phrase wayáwa tí (school, literally "reading/counting house"), showing how compound nouns preserve historical moments.

docs.title: Section 2 — Verb Conjugation
docs.text:
Grammar: Active Verb Conjugation

Dakota active verbs mark the subject with infixed or prefixed personal markers. For most active verbs, the pattern is:

Person Prefix/Infix Example (yúta = to eat) I (1sg) wa- wayúta — I eat You (2sg) ya- yayúta — you eat He/She (3sg) (none) yúta — he/she eats We (1pl incl.) uŋ-...-pi uŋyútapi — we (all) eat You all (2pl) ya-...-pi yayútapi — you all eat They (3pl) -pi yútapi — they eat

Note: The -pi suffix marks plural for all persons. The verb root stays the same; prefixes and suffixes do the work.

docs.title: Section 3 — Future Tense and Negation
docs.text:
Grammar: Future Tense with -kte

The suffix -kte attaches to the end of a verb (after any other suffixes) to express future intention or prediction:

  • Wayúta. → I eat. (present)
  • Wayúta kte. → I will eat. (future)
  • Yápi kte. → They will go. (future plural)

-kte is not an auxiliary verb — it is a suffix that bonds to the verb. It can follow the plural -pi suffix: yápi kte (they will go).

Grammar: Negation with -šni

The suffix -šni attaches to negate a verb:

  • Wayúta šni. → I do not eat. / I am not eating.
  • Wayúta kte šni. → I will not eat. (future negation: -kte comes before -šni)
  • Yápi kte šni. → They will not go.

The order is always: verb root + -kte (if future) + -šni (negation)

AIS 112 Connection: The Tipi as Living Architecture

The word tipi literally means "dwelling" (ti = to dwell, pi = plural marker making it a noun of habitation). The conical buffalo-hide tipi was not a primitive shelter but a sophisticated, portable, climate-responsive dwelling. It could be erected in under an hour, packed onto a travois, and moved with the seasonal migration of the bison herds. The tipi's circular interior had specific zones: the area opposite the entrance was honored space for elders and guests; the fire at center was both heat source and sacred focus. When tipi entered English as "tepee," it lost all of this architectural and social meaning. In Dakota, the word still carries it.

Exercise 1: Reorder into SOV

Rewrite these English-order sentences into correct Dakota SOV order (Dakota words provided, just reorder):

  1. English: "The woman eats the berry." Words: wičhíŋčala (woman), čhaŋpá šápa (chokecherry), yúta (eats)
  2. English: "The child will go to school." Words: čhiŋkší (child), wayáwa tí (school), blé kte (will go)
  3. English: "They do not read." Words: wayáwapi šni (they do not read)

Remember: Subject → Object → Verb.

Exercise 2: Conjugate the Verb

Conjugate the verb hí (to come/arrive) for all six persons (I, you, he/she, we, you all, they). Then add -kte for future tense to each form.

Using the vocabulary from this chapter, build five complete Dakota sentences — at least two in future tense and one negative. Include subjects, objects, and verbs in SOV order. Write each Dakota sentence with its English translation.

Example: Wiŋyaŋ kiŋ wóyute kiŋ wayúta kte šni. — The woman will not eat the food.

Chapter 3 Quiz

docs.title: Chapter 3 Quiz — Wóuŋsipi: Daily Life & Action Verbs
Part A — Multiple Choice (10 questions, 2 points each)
docs.text:
1. What does the acronym SOV refer to in Dakota grammar? Answer

b) Subject-Object-Verb

Dakota is an SOV language: the subject comes first, then the object, and the verb comes last. This contrasts with English SVO order (Subject-Verb-Object). Example: Wiŋyaŋ kiŋ wóyute kiŋ yúta. = "The woman the food eats" (The woman eats the food).

a) Subject-Verb-Object b) Subject-Object-Verb c) Object-Subject-Verb d) Verb-Subject-Object

2. Which suffix is used to form the future tense in Dakota? Answer

c) -kte

-kte is the future tense suffix in Dakota. It attaches after the verb root (and after -pi if plural). Example: wayúta kte = "I will eat." This differs from Ojibwe, which uses a future prefix rather than a suffix.

a) -šni b) -pi c) -kte d) -la

3. What does the negation suffix -šni do, and where does it appear relative to -kte? Answer

b) It negates the verb; it appears AFTER -kte in future negative sentences

The suffix -šni negates a verb. In a future negative sentence, the order is: verb + -kte + -šni. Example: wayúta kte šni = "I will not eat." Never place -šni before -kte.

a) It marks plural; it appears before -kte b) It negates the verb; it appears AFTER -kte in future negative sentences c) It negates the verb; it appears BEFORE -kte d) It marks question form; it appears after the verb

4. How do you say 'I eat' in Dakota using the verb yúta? Answer

a) wayúta

The first-person singular active prefix is wa-, attached to the verb root yúta: wa-yúta = "I eat." Note the wa- prefix is an indefinite-object or first-person active marker.

a) wayúta b) yayúta c) uŋyútapi d) yútapi

5. What is the correct Dakota word order for 'The man reads the book'? Answer

c) Wičhášta kiŋ wówapi kiŋ wayáwa.

SOV order places the verb last: Subject (Wičhášta kiŋ = the man) + Object (wówapi kiŋ = the book) + Verb (wayáwa = reads/counts). Options a and b use English SVO order; option d incorrectly places kiŋ at the start.

a) Wičhášta kiŋ wayáwa wówapi kiŋ. b) Wayáwa wičhášta kiŋ wówapi kiŋ. c) Wičhášta kiŋ wówapi kiŋ wayáwa. d) Kiŋ wičhášta wówapi wayáwa.

6. What does wayáwa tí mean literally, and what does it refer to? Answer

b) "Reading/counting house" — it means school

wayáwa = to read/count; tí = dwelling/house. wayáwa tí = "the house where one reads/counts" = school. This compound reveals the history of how Dakota communities encountered formal literacy as an extension of the counting practice they already had.

a) "Story house" — it means library b) "Reading/counting house" — it means school c) "Prayer house" — it means church d) "Eating house" — it means kitchen

7. In Dakota, uŋyútapi means: Answer

c) We eat (inclusive plural)

uŋ-yúta-pi: the prefix uŋ- marks first-person plural inclusive (we, including the listener); the suffix -pi marks plurality. This form implies "we — you and I and others — eat together." The inclusive/exclusive distinction is grammatically significant in Dakota.

a) You all eat b) They eat c) We eat (inclusive plural) d) I am eating

8. The verb hí means: Answer

a) to come / to arrive (toward the speaker)

hí means "to come" or "to arrive," specifically with a directional implication of movement toward the speaker's location. Its counterpart yá means "to go" — movement away from the speaker. This directional distinction is common in Dakota verbs of motion.

a) to come / to arrive (toward the speaker) b) to go / to leave (away from speaker) c) to be / to exist d) to stand

9. Which Dakota word means 'morning'? Answer

b) híŋhaŋna

híŋhaŋna = morning. haŋhépi = night, aŋpétu = day, iyókaptan = afternoon. These time words are frequently used in daily-life sentence construction.

a) haŋhépi b) híŋhaŋna c) aŋpétu d) iyókaptan

10. According to the AIS 112 content in this chapter, what does the word tipi literally mean? Answer

c) Dwelling / place to live

tipi comes from ti- (to dwell) + -pi (a nominalizing plural suffix). It means "dwelling" or "the place where one lives." The conical buffalo-hide lodge was a sophisticated, portable, climate-responsive architecture — not merely a "tent" as English simplifications suggest.

a) Circle of fire b) Buffalo house c) Dwelling / place to live d) Family gathering place

docs.title: Part B — Fill in the Blank (3 questions, 5 points each)
docs.text:
11. To say 'They will not go' in Dakota, you write: yápi ____ šni. Answer

kte

Yápi kte šni. = They will not go. The order is always: verb (+ plural -pi) + future -kte + negation -šni. Placing -šni before -kte would be a grammatical error.

12. The first-person singular prefix for most active Dakota verbs is: ____ Answer

wa-

The prefix wa- marks the first person singular as the active subject for most transitive verbs. Example: wa-yúta (I eat), wa-yáwa (I read/count). Some common verbs like yá (to go) use irregular contracted forms (blé for "I go").

13. The word wayáwa originally meant ____ before it expanded to include the meaning 'to read.' Answer

to count / to reckon

wayáwa originally meant "to count" or "to reckon numbers." The semantic expansion to "to read" reflects Dakota communities' encounter with written text — reading was understood as a kind of counting or reckoning of symbols.

docs.title: Part C — Short Answer (3 questions, 10 points each)
docs.text:
14. Construct three complete Dakota sentences using SOV word order. One must be in future tense, one must be negative, and one must be a question. Label each and provide English translations. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): All three sentences are grammatically correct, exhibit SOV order, and clearly demonstrate future -kte, negation -šni, and question particle he?. English translations are accurate.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Two of the three sentences are correct; third has a minor error (e.g., wrong word order, missing particle).

Sample answers:

Future: Wiŋyaŋ kiŋ wóyute kiŋ wayúta kte. — The woman will eat the food.

Negative: Čhiŋkší kiŋ wayáwa šni. — The child does not read.

Question: Wičhášta kiŋ hí he? — Did the man come? / Is the man arriving?

15. Explain the inclusive/exclusive 'we' distinction in Dakota verb conjugation. Why is this distinction linguistically and culturally significant? Give an example. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately explains that Dakota distinguishes between "we including the listener" (inclusive) and "we not including the listener" (exclusive) through different verb prefixes. Student provides a culturally grounded reflection (e.g., the value of wóčhekiye/relatedness means that whether you include or exclude someone from a group action matters) and gives a grammatically correct example.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student explains the linguistic distinction correctly but does not connect it to cultural values, or vice versa.

Sample answer: "Dakota grammar distinguishes whether 'we' includes the person being spoken to (inclusive: uŋ-...-pi) or excludes them (exclusive: a different form). In English, 'we' is ambiguous — it might or might not include you. In Dakota, this ambiguity is unacceptable. The language forces the speaker to be precise about who is included in collective action. This reflects the Dakota value of wóčhekiye — relatedness — and the communal structure of the tiyóšpaye, where knowing exactly who shares in an action is socially and practically important. Example: Uŋyútapi means 'we eat' in a way that includes the listener — all of us together eat."

16. What is the cultural and historical significance of the fact that the Dakota word wayáwa expanded from 'to count' to include 'to read'? What does this tell us about how Dakota communities encountered literacy? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student explains that wayáwa preserves a historical moment — the encounter with written text — within the language itself. Student reflects on what it means for a community to map a new practice onto an existing cognitive category (counting → reading), and may connect this to broader themes of indigenous language adaptation and resilience.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student identifies the historical fact but does not reflect on its deeper implications for language, history, or cultural adaptation.

Sample answer: "The expansion of wayáwa from 'to count' to 'to read' is a linguistic fossil — it preserves the exact moment when Dakota-speaking communities first encountered written text and tried to make sense of it. Rather than borrowing a foreign word for 'read,' Dakota speakers understood the new practice through an existing cognitive frame: reckoning symbols, as one reckons numbers. This is an act of cultural translation embedded in the language itself. It also tells us that Dakota was a living, adaptive language — not frozen in pre-contact form but actively incorporating new realities while maintaining its own conceptual categories. The compound wayáwa tí (school) extends this further, showing how the language kept growing through contact without losing its structural identity."

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Chapter 4 introduces Dakota vocabulary for body parts, health, emotions, and kinship. Students encounter one of Dakota's most complex and culturally significant systems: the kinship terminology, which varies by the speaker's gender and encodes relationship through social role rather than biological category alone. AIS 112 content addresses Dakota family structures, the role of kinship in community survival, and how the destruction of kinship networks was central to colonial policies targeting Dakota people.

docs.title: AIS 112 Cultural Context — Weeks 7–9
docs.text:
Kinship as the Foundation of Dakota Society

For Dakota people, kinship (wótakuye) is not merely a family tree — it is the organizing principle of all social, political, and spiritual life. Before you speak to someone, you establish relationship. Every Dakota social interaction begins with knowing: who are you to me, and who am I to you? This is why Dakota kinship terminology is so precise — it must carry the weight of social organization.

The kinship system distinguishes not just uncle from aunt, but which uncle or aunt, from whose side, and crucially: who is speaking. A woman and a man use different words for "sister" because sisterhood is experienced differently depending on gender role. This is not sexism — it is precision about the social weight of a relationship.

Colonial Disruption of Kinship

One of the most devastating effects of the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, the subsequent forced removal, and the allotment era was the systematic destruction of kinship networks. Children removed to boarding schools were forbidden from speaking Dakota and were cut off from the extended family structures that transmitted the language. The loss of kinship vocabulary — the very words for grandmother, cousin, sister — was therefore not incidental to colonization; it was one of its primary instruments. Revitalizing this vocabulary is an act of cultural restoration.

The Body as Sacred Geography

In Dakota thought, the body (čhaŋté — heart, the core of selfhood) is a sacred geography. The heart is the center, not the head. Wisdom, courage, love — these qualities are not cognitive but cardiac, rooted in the heart. This is why čhaŋté appears in so many compound words: čhaŋtéčhila (love, "heart-small/dear"), čhantéčhilapi (we love you), čhantéyapi (beloved).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
In English, the word "sister" is one word. In Dakota, it depends on who is speaking. A woman speaking of her sister uses čhuwítkala. A man speaking of his sister uses čhaŋkší. These are not the same word — they encode two different social relationships, two different sets of responsibilities and emotional weights.

This is the nature of Dakota kinship terminology: it is not a labeling system but a relational system. Every kinship term encodes the speaker's position as well as the referent's position. It tells you not just who the person is, but who they are to you, and who you are to them.

The body, in Dakota, is understood through the same relational lens. The word čhaŋté — heart — is not just the organ that pumps blood. It is the seat of the self, the center of courage, love, and grief. When you learn Dakota body vocabulary, you learn a map of what Dakota culture considers essential in a human being.

The metaphor is arboreal: Dakota people, who lived in the forests and prairies of Minnesota, drew their image of interior strength from the trees around them.

Grammar: The Verb of Pain — mayázaŋ

yázaŋ is a verb meaning "to ache, to hurt, to be painful." It takes an object prefix to indicate who is experiencing the pain:

  • Čhaŋté mayázaŋ. → My heart aches. (I am sad / grieving)
  • Naté niyázaŋ he? → Is your head hurting? (Do you have a headache?)
  • Síha čhiyázaŋ. → Your foot hurts.

This construction models an important Dakota grammatical pattern: the body part is the subject, and the person experiencing pain takes an object-position prefix on the verb.

docs.title: Section 3 — Kinship Terms
docs.text:
AIS 112 Connection: Kinship and Identity

In traditional Dakota society, you introduced yourself by naming your tiyóšpaye and your kin relationships — not your individual name first. Kinship terms were the vocabulary of identity. When missionaries and government officials began recording Dakota names in the 1800s, they often recorded only individual names, erasing the kinship layer that gave those names their social meaning.

Grammar: Possessive Kinship Terms

Kinship terms take the same possessive prefixes as body parts:

  • mi-čhuwítkala → my (younger) sister (female speaking)

In Dakota speech, kinship terms are frequently used without possessive prefixes when the context is clear — "čhuwítkala hí" can mean "my sister arrived" if the speaker is female and context implies it.

Chapter 4 Quiz

docs.title: Chapter 4 Quiz — Čhaŋté: Body, Health & Relationships
Part A — Multiple Choice (10 questions, 2 points each)
docs.text:
1. What does the word čhaŋté mean in Dakota? Answer

b) Heart

čhaŋté means heart and is the center of Dakota selfhood — courage, love, and grief are located here, not in the head. It appears in many compound words: čhaŋtéčhila (love/beloved), čhantéčhilapi (we love you).

a) Head b) Heart c) Hand d) Soul

2. A female Dakota speaker uses which word to refer to her younger sister? Answer

a) čhuwítkala

čhuwítkala is the term a female speaker uses for her (younger) sister. A male speaker uses čhaŋkší for his sister. This speaker-gender distinction is fundamental to Dakota kinship vocabulary.

a) čhuwítkala b) čhaŋkší c) šičhéši d) haŋká

3. What does čhaŋté mayázaŋ mean? Answer

c) My heart aches / I am grieving

čhaŋté = heart; ma-yázaŋ = it hurts me (ma- = me, yázaŋ = to ache). The construction places the body part as the grammatical subject and the experiencer as an object prefix on the verb. It expresses both physical heart pain and emotional grief.

a) Your heart is strong b) The heart is red c) My heart aches / I am grieving d) I have no heart

4. The Dakota word pežúta primarily means: Answer

b) Medicine / medicinal plant

pežúta means medicine or medicinal herb — literally it is related to the word for grass/plant, emphasizing that traditional Dakota medicine came from plant knowledge. pežúta wiŋyaŋ = medicine woman; wičhášta wakan = holy man/medicine man.

a) Doctor b) Medicine / medicinal plant c) Sickness d) Ceremony

5. What is the possessive prefix meaning 'my' used with body parts and kinship terms in Dakota? Answer

a) mi- / ma-

The first-person possessive prefix is mi- (sometimes ma- depending on the following vowel and phonological environment). Examples: mičhaŋté (my heart), minape (my hand), mičhuwítkala (my sister, female speaking).

a) mi- / ma- b) ni- c) ta- d) wa-

6. What does šičhéši mean? Answer

c) Male cousin (cross-cousin)

šičhéši refers to a male cousin, specifically a cross-cousin in the Dakota kinship system. The cross-cousin relationship (father's sister's child or mother's brother's child) had specific social roles in Dakota society distinct from parallel cousins.

a) Older brother b) Father's brother c) Male cousin (cross-cousin) d) Grandfather

7. According to the chapter, why is the body part čhaŋté (heart) etymologically connected to the word for 'tree' (čháŋ)? Answer

b) The heart is understood as the innermost core, like the heartwood of a tree

čhaŋté contains the root čháŋ (tree/wood) and implies the innermost core — the "heartwood." Just as the strength of a tree lies in its inner rings, a person's strength comes from their čhaŋté. This arboreal metaphor reflects the Dakota world of northern forests and plains.

a) The heart pumps blood like sap in a tree b) The heart is understood as the innermost core, like the heartwood of a tree c) Trees were used to make medicine for heart conditions d) Both words share a sound but have no etymological connection

8. Which term is used to address a grandmother respectfully in Dakota? Answer

c) uŋčí

uŋčí is the Dakota word for grandmother and term of respectful direct address. tȟuŋkášila = grandfather (and also used for the Great Spirit in prayer). até = father; thimá = mother.

a) tȟuŋkášila b) até c) uŋčí d) haŋká

9. To say 'I am well' in Dakota, you would say: Answer

b) Waníčiŋ waúŋ.

Waníčiŋ = to be well/healthy; waúŋ = I am/I exist. Together: "I am in a state of wellness." The opposite is wayázaŋka waúŋ (I am sick).

a) Mayázaŋ waúŋ. b) Waníčiŋ waúŋ. c) Pežúta waúŋ. d) Šni waúŋ.

10. According to the AIS 112 cultural content, how was the destruction of kinship networks used as a colonial tool? Answer

b) Children in boarding schools were forbidden to speak Dakota and were separated from extended family, erasing the kinship vocabulary that transmitted cultural identity

The systematic removal of children to boarding schools — where they were forbidden to speak Dakota and were isolated from their tiyóšpaye — directly attacked the kinship system. Since kinship terms are the vocabulary of Dakota identity (who you are = who you belong to), erasing these words was a strategy of cultural erasure.

a) The government outlawed the use of kinship terms in legal documents b) Children in boarding schools were forbidden to speak Dakota and were separated from extended family, erasing the kinship vocabulary that transmitted cultural identity c) Missionaries replaced kinship terms with Christian family vocabulary d) Allotment divided kinship groups onto separate land parcels, but language was not affected

docs.title: Part B — Fill in the Blank (3 questions, 5 points each)
docs.text:
11. The Dakota word for 'eye' is _, and 'my eye' is _. Answer
  • Eye: išta
  • My eye: míšta (or miišta)

The possessive is formed with mi- prefix: mi- + išta = míšta. When the noun begins with a vowel, the mi- prefix often contracts: míšta, mí (my mouth, from í).

12. A male speaker refers to his sister as _, while a female speaker uses _ for the same relationship. Answer
  • Male speaker: čhaŋkší
  • Female speaker: čhuwítkala

This is one of the most important kinship distinctions in this chapter. The difference reflects not just biological relation but social role: a man's sister occupies a different relational position in his life than a woman's sister occupies in hers.

13. In the pain construction, naté niyázaŋ, the prefix ni- means _ and the overall phrase means _. Answer
  • ni- = you / your (second person object prefix)
  • Phrase meaning: Your head hurts / Do you have a headache?

naté = head; ni-yázaŋ = it hurts you. The verb yázaŋ takes an object-position person prefix to indicate the experiencer of the pain.

docs.title: Part C — Short Answer (3 questions, 10 points each)
docs.text:
14. Explain the concept of wótakuye (kinship) as the organizing principle of Dakota society. How does this concept help explain why Dakota kinship terminology is more complex than English kinship terminology? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately explains wótakuye as a social, political, and spiritual organizing principle (not merely biological family). Student connects this to the precision of Dakota kinship terms (speaker-gender distinctions, cross-cousin vs. parallel cousin distinctions, etc.) and explains why English's simpler kinship vocabulary cannot capture the same social information.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student describes kinship as important but does not explain the structural connection between social organization and terminological complexity.

Sample answer: "Wótakuye is the Dakota concept of kinship as total social relationship — it determines your obligations, your alliances, your spiritual connections, and your identity. Because kinship organizes everything, the language needs precise vocabulary to encode all the relevant distinctions. English 'sister' is one word because English society doesn't require knowing, from the word itself, who is speaking. Dakota requires this because the social weight of the relationship differs by the speaker's position: a man's obligation to his sister is different from a woman's obligation to hers, and the language encodes this distinction in the words themselves."

15. Describe the mayázaŋ construction in Dakota grammar. How does this construction differ from English expressions of pain, and what does it reveal about Dakota grammatical priorities? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately describes the construction ([body part] + [person prefix + yázaŋ]), contrasts it with English ("my head hurts" vs. "I have a headache"), and reflects on what it means to treat the body part as the grammatical subject acting upon the experiencer.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student describes the construction correctly but does not reflect on grammatical implications.

Sample answer: "In English, we say 'I have a headache' or 'my head hurts' — the person is usually the subject. In Dakota, the mayázaŋ construction places the body part as the grammatical subject and the experiencer as an object prefix on the verb: Naté mayázaŋ = 'The head hurts me / My head hurts.' The body part does the acting; the person receives the experience. This reflects a Dakota grammatical tendency to distribute agency — the head is not merely passive; it is doing something to me. This construction appears consistently in health vocabulary and reveals how Dakota grammar encodes a relational, intersubjective view of the body."

16. How did U.S. colonial policies — specifically the boarding school system — target Dakota kinship as a tool of cultural erasure? Connect your answer to at least two specific vocabulary items from this chapter. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately describes the boarding school system's role in separating children from tiyóšpaye, forbidding Dakota language, and thereby severing the transmission of kinship vocabulary. Student references at least two specific terms (e.g., čhuwítkala, uŋčí, tȟuŋkášila, haŋká, etc.) and explains how losing these words meant losing the relationships they named.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student identifies the boarding school system and language prohibition but makes only general reference to kinship vocabulary.

Sample answer: "The boarding school system — which removed Dakota children from their communities beginning in the 1870s and intensifying after 1880 — explicitly forbade children from speaking Dakota. Children who arrived still knowing words like uŋčí (grandmother) or čhuwítkala (younger sister, female speaking) were punished for using them. Within a generation, children returned home unable to address their own grandmothers correctly — they had lost not just words but the relational knowledge those words encoded. Uŋčí is not just a label; it is a set of responsibilities, stories, and prayers that flow between a grandmother and grandchild. Losing uŋčí meant losing access to that entire relational universe. The same is true of terms like tȟuŋkášila (grandfather), which also appears in sacred prayer — to lose it was to lose access to spiritual tradition. This is why linguistic revitalization is inseparable from cultural healing."

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Wóčhekiye: Prayer, Values & The Sacred
Summary
docs.text: Chapter 5 introduces the vocabulary of Dakota spiritual life — prayer, sacred values, and core ethical concepts. Students learn the phrase Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ (all my relations), the four cardinal virtues of Dakota life, and vocabulary for ceremony and the sacred. AIS 112 content examines how Dakota spiritual practice was criminalized under U.S. law and how its suppression was inseparable from the broader dispossession of Dakota people.

docs.title: AIS 112 Cultural Context — Weeks 9–11
docs.text:
Dakota Spiritual Life and the Four Virtues

Traditional Dakota spiritual life was not a separate "religion" compartmentalized from daily activity — it was woven through every aspect of living. The four cardinal virtues — wačháŋtognaka (generosity), ohítika (bravery), ksapá (wisdom), and čhaŋtéčhila (love) — were not personal aspirations but communal responsibilities. A person who embodied these virtues did not merely improve themselves; they strengthened the entire tiyóšpaye.

These virtues were demonstrated publicly through give-aways (wóhanpi), acts of protection, council deliberation, and the raising of children. The person who gave away the most was honored more than the person who accumulated the most.

Criminalization of Dakota Ceremony

Between 1883 and 1934, the U.S. government enforced the Code of Indian Offenses, which made many Dakota spiritual practices illegal — including the Sun Dance, traditional ceremony, and the practices of medicine people. This was not incidental to colonization; it was deliberate cultural and spiritual assault. Dakota people continued their practices in secret, at great personal risk. The American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 finally restored legal protections, though enforcement has remained inconsistent.

Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ

The phrase Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ — often translated as "all my relations" or "we are all related" — is one of the most widely known expressions from Lakota/Dakota spiritual tradition. It opens and closes ceremony; it is spoken at the end of prayer; it is an acknowledgment that the speaker exists in relationship with all living beings — human, animal, plant, and spirit. It is not a greeting; it is a declaration of relationship.

docs.text: Chapter 4 — Čhaŋté. Students should be comfortable with stative verbs, kinship vocabulary, and the čhaŋté (heart) as a conceptual root in Dakota language.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The word wóčhekiye means prayer — but the Dakota concept of prayer is broader than most English speakers expect. Wóčhekiye is not only formal petition to a deity. It is the ongoing practice of maintaining relationship with all that is sacred: the land, the ancestors, the living community, and the mystery that animates everything. When a Dakota elder says Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ, they are not merely being polite. They are asserting an entire cosmological position: that they exist in web of relationship with all life.

The four virtues — generosity, bravery, wisdom, love — are not passive traits in Dakota culture. They are active practices, demonstrated daily and publicly. The most admired person in a Dakota community was not the wealthiest or the most powerful but the most generous — the one who gave away their own goods so that others would not suffer. Wačháŋtognaka is often translated as generosity, but it carries deeper weight: the act of expanding your heart outward, beyond yourself, toward the whole community.

The language of Dakota spirituality is also the language of resistance. When Dakota communities maintained their ceremonies in secret during the years of prohibition, they were not merely preserving cultural traditions — they were refusing the colonial demand that they cease to exist as a people.

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka
docs.text:
Break down the name for the Great Spirit Morpheme Meaning Wakȟáŋ sacred, mysterious, beyond ordinary comprehension Tȟáŋka great, large, vast

Analysis: Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka is often translated as "Great Spirit" in English, but this translation misses something important. Wakȟáŋ does not simply mean "spiritual" — it means mysterious, beyond ordinary knowing, charged with power. The word is used for electricity, for the steam locomotive (which early Dakota people called mázawakȟáŋ — mysterious iron), for sacred ceremony. Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka is therefore not just a "great spirit" but the Great Mystery — the ultimate unknowable source of all that is charged with power. This is a more philosophically precise (and humbler) translation.

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ
docs.text:
Break down "all my relations" Morpheme Meaning mi- my / mine (first person possessive) -tákuye relations, relatives (takuya = to be related to) oyásʼiŋ all, every one

Analysis: The full phrase is Mi-tákuye Oyásʼiŋ — literally "all those related to me" or "all my relations." The mi- possessive is crucial: this is not "all relations" in general, but my relations — a personal declaration of belonging. The speaker claims kinship with everything: human, animal, plant, and spirit. This is the Dakota cosmological statement that the self is not separate from the world but woven into it.

AIS 112 Connection: The Suppression of Ceremony

The inípi (sweat lodge) and the wiwáŋyag wačhípi (Sun Dance) were specifically targeted by the 1883 Code of Indian Offenses. Violation could result in imprisonment, withholding of rations, and other punishments. Yet Dakota and Lakota communities continued these practices — often in secret, often at night — because they understood that without ceremony, the community could not survive. The revival of these practices after 1978 (American Indian Religious Freedom Act) was therefore not a nostalgic recovery but a continuation of resistance that had never fully stopped.

In 2–3 sentences in English (this is a reflection exercise, not translation): - How does the phrase Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ challenge individualistic assumptions about the self? - How does the virtue of wačháŋtognaka (generosity) differ from its Western equivalent? - What does it mean for a language to encode spiritual values directly in its vocabulary?
