docs.title: Chapter 5 Quiz — Wóčhekiye: Prayer, Values & The Sacred
Part A — Multiple Choice (10 questions, 2 points each)
docs.text:
1. What is the most accurate English translation of Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ? Answer

b) All my relations / we are all related

Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ breaks down as mi- (my) + tákuye (relations) + oyásʼiŋ (all). It is a personal declaration of kinship with all living beings. "All my relations" captures the possessive mi- better than "all relations" does.

a) I am sacred b) All my relations / we are all related c) Great Spirit, hear me d) We are one people

2. The Dakota word wakan is best translated as: Answer

c) Sacred, mysterious, charged with power

wakan covers a range English splits into many words: sacred, mysterious, spiritually powerful, beyond ordinary comprehension. It was used for electricity, steam engines, and ceremony alike — anything that exceeds ordinary knowing.

a) Holy man b) Prayer c) Sacred, mysterious, charged with power d) Ancestor spirit

3. Which of the four cardinal Dakota virtues is best described as 'expanding one's heart outward toward the community'? Answer

a) wačháŋtognaka (generosity)

wačháŋtognaka — generosity — is the most socially central virtue. In Dakota culture, the most honored person gave away the most. The word itself contains čhaŋté (heart) and connotes placing one's heart-resources outward toward others.

a) wačháŋtognaka (generosity) b) ohítika (bravery) c) ksapá (wisdom) d) čhaŋtéčhila (love)

4. What law, passed in 1883, made many Dakota spiritual practices illegal? Answer

b) The Code of Indian Offenses

The Code of Indian Offenses (1883) targeted the Sun Dance, traditional ceremony, and the practices of medicine people. Violation could result in imprisonment and withholding of rations. This was reversed by the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978.

a) The Indian Removal Act b) The Code of Indian Offenses c) The Dawes Act d) The Indian Civilization Act

5. How do you say 'I will be brave' in Dakota? Answer

c) Ohítika waúŋ kte.

ohítika (bravery/brave, stative verb) + waúŋ (I am/exist) + kte (future suffix) = "I will be in a state of bravery." The stative verb pattern requires waúŋ to link the virtue to the first person.

a) Ohítika yá kte. b) Ohítika waúŋ šni. c) Ohítika waúŋ kte. d) Waúŋ ohítika kte.

6. What is inípi? Answer

b) The sweat lodge purification ceremony

inípi is the Dakota/Lakota sweat lodge ceremony, used for purification of body and spirit. It was one of the ceremonies specifically targeted by the 1883 Code of Indian Offenses. iní = to take a sweat bath.

a) A sacred pipe b) The sweat lodge purification ceremony c) A give-away feast d) A winter prayer ceremony

7. The word čheyáka refers to which ceremonial plant? Answer

a) Sage

čheyáka = sage, used in smudging and purification rituals. čhaŋšášayapi or čháŋšaša is kinnikinnick (red willow bark), used in the sacred pipe mixture. These two plants are distinct but both important in ceremony.

a) Sage b) Cedar c) Sweetgrass d) Red willow

8. Which word means 'wisdom' as a Dakota cardinal virtue? Answer

c) ksapá

ksapá = wisdom, specifically practical wisdom earned through experience and listening. It is one of the four cardinal virtues alongside wačháŋtognaka (generosity), ohítika (bravery), and čhaŋtéčhila (love).

a) wačháŋtognaka b) ohítika c) ksapá d) wóčhekiye

9. Why is Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka better translated as 'Great Mystery' than 'Great Spirit'? Answer

b) Because wakan means "mysterious/beyond ordinary knowing" — not just "spiritual" — and "Mystery" better captures this sense of the unknowable

wakȟáŋ covers electricity, steam locomotives, and sacred ceremony — anything that exceeds ordinary comprehension. "Great Spirit" imports a Western personified deity concept that does not match the Dakota philosophical meaning. "Great Mystery" is more philosophically accurate.

a) Because the Dakota did not believe in spirits b) Because wakan means "mysterious/beyond ordinary knowing" — not just "spiritual" — and "Mystery" better captures this sense of the unknowable c) Because the word tȟáŋka means mystery, not greatness d) Because missionaries introduced the translation "Great Spirit" as a conversion tool and it is therefore colonial

10. In what year did the American Indian Religious Freedom Act restore legal protections for Native ceremonial practices? Answer

c) 1978

The American Indian Religious Freedom Act was signed in 1978, nearly a century after the 1883 Code of Indian Offenses criminalized many Dakota and other indigenous spiritual practices. However, enforcement has remained inconsistent since 1978.

a) 1934 b) 1968 c) 1978 d) 1990

docs.title: Part B — Fill in the Blank (3 questions, 5 points each)
docs.text:
11. The Dakota word for prayer — the ongoing practice of maintaining relationship with all that is sacred — is ____. Answer

wóčhekiye

wóčhekiye is both a noun (prayer, an act of prayer) and describes the practice of relational prayerfulness. It is broader than the English "prayer," encompassing ongoing relationship with the sacred rather than only formal petition.

12. Complete the sentence: Wičhášta kiŋ ksapá ____. (The man is wise.) Answer

The sentence Wičhášta kiŋ ksapá is already complete as a predicate construction.

However, if the exercise asks for the existential verb to make the predicate explicit: waúŋ → Wičhášta kiŋ ksapá waúŋ. — The man exists in a state of wisdom.

(Note: in Dakota, stative verbs like ksapá can stand alone as predicates without a linking verb; waúŋ makes the construction more explicit.)

13. The four cardinal Dakota virtues are: _, _, _, and _. Answer
  1. wačháŋtognaka (generosity)
  2. ohítika (bravery)
  3. ksapá (wisdom)
  4. čhaŋtéčhila (love / cherishing)

These four virtues were publicly demonstrated through community action — give-aways, acts of protection, council wisdom, and the raising of children with care.

docs.title: Part C — Short Answer (3 questions, 10 points each)
docs.text:
14. Explain the full Dakota meaning of Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ — including its morpheme breakdown — and describe how its ceremonial use expresses a Dakota view of selfhood that differs from Western individualism. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student provides accurate morpheme breakdown (mi- + tákuye + oyásʼiŋ), correct translation, and a substantive reflection on how the phrase encodes a relational, non-individualistic view of the self — one that claims kinship with all life, not just human community.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Correct breakdown and translation but shallow or absent reflection on the philosophical/cultural dimension.

Sample answer: "Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ breaks down as mi- (my/mine) + tákuye (relations, from takuya = to be related to) + oyásʼiŋ (all, every one). The full meaning is 'all those related to me' or 'all my relations.' The possessive mi- is essential: the speaker is not making a general philosophical statement about the universe — they are declaring personal kinship with all living beings. This challenges Western individualism, which treats the self as a bounded, autonomous unit. The Dakota self, as expressed in Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ, is relationally constituted — you exist because you are in relationship. The phrase closes ceremony as a reminder that every prayer, every action, every word ripples outward into all these relationships."

15. Describe the role of the four cardinal virtues (wačháŋtognaka, ohítika, ksapá, čhaŋtéčhila) in traditional Dakota communal life. How were these virtues demonstrated publicly, and what does this reveal about the relationship between individual virtue and communal health? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately describes all four virtues and their communal — not merely individual — expression. Student explains at least one form of public demonstration (give-away, battle protection, council deliberation, child-raising) and reflects on how individual virtue strengthened the tiyóšpaye.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student describes virtues correctly but focuses only on individual dimension without connecting to communal health.

Sample answer: "The four cardinal virtues were not private moral qualities in Dakota culture — they were communal responsibilities demonstrated through action. Wačháŋtognaka (generosity) was shown through the wóhanpi give-away, where a family distributed goods to the community; the most generous person was most honored. Ohítika (bravery) was not recklessness but deliberate courage in protection of the tiyóšpaye — demonstrated in battle and in speaking difficult truths in council. Ksapá (wisdom) was earned through decades of listening and experience; elders who possessed it were consulted on all major decisions. Čhaŋtéčhila (love/cherishing) was demonstrated through the raising of children and the care of elders. Together, these virtues operated as the connective tissue of community health. A person who was truly generous, brave, wise, and loving strengthened the entire band — and their honored status reflected this communal benefit."

16. What was the Code of Indian Offenses (1883), what specific Dakota practices did it target, and what forms of resistance did Dakota communities use to maintain their spiritual traditions? Connect your answer to at least two vocabulary items from this chapter. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately describes the Code of Indian Offenses, names at least two targeted practices, describes at least one form of resistance (continuation in secret, at night, etc.), and connects to at least two vocabulary items from Chapter 5 (e.g., inípi, wiwáŋyag wačhípi, čheyáka, wóčhekiye).

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Accurate description of the Code but weak connection to vocabulary, or strong vocabulary connection but incomplete description of resistance.

Sample answer: "The Code of Indian Offenses was a set of federal regulations enacted in 1883 that criminalized many indigenous spiritual and cultural practices. Specifically, it targeted the Sun Dance (wiwáŋyag wačhípi — 'dance looking at the sun'), the inípi (sweat lodge purification ceremony), and the practices of medicine people. Violations could result in imprisonment and the withholding of rations — a devastating punishment for communities already deprived of their land and subsistence base. Yet Dakota communities did not abandon these practices. They continued inípi ceremonies in hidden locations, maintained wóčhekiye (prayer) privately within families, and passed down knowledge of čheyáka (sage) and its ceremonial uses through trusted networks. This resistance was not passive — it was active cultural survival, maintained at personal risk across nearly a century until the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 restored legal protections."

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Chapter 6 introduces Dakota vocabulary for the land, the four seasons, the cardinal directions, and the moon-based calendar. Students learn how Dakota encodes relationship to place — not as property or backdrop, but as living relationship — and how the seasonal calendar structures knowledge, ceremony, and language. AIS 112 content addresses the significance of the land (makóčhe) in Dakota sovereignty and the impact of treaty violations on Dakota people's relationship to their homeland.

docs.title: AIS 112 Cultural Context — Weeks 11–13
docs.text:
Makóčhe — Land as Living Relationship

The Dakota word makóčhe is often translated simply as "land" or "country," but its meaning is deeper. Maka = earth/land; čhe suggests interior or essential nature. Makóčhe is the land as homeland — not merely geography, but the living ground of identity, memory, and spiritual practice. For the Dakota people, specific places — lakes, rivers, hills, forests — are not scenery but relatives, inhabited by specific spirits and anchored in specific histories.

The Dakota heartland — Bdóte (the confluence of the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers, near present-day Fort Snelling) — was considered the center of the Dakota world. It was the place of creation in Dakota oral tradition. When the U.S. government seized this land and built Fort Snelling on it, the violation was not merely political — it was ontological, an assault on the center of Dakota being.

Treaty Violations and Land Loss

The 1851 treaties of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota — signed under enormous pressure and in some cases fraud — stripped the Dakota people of most of their Minnesota homeland in exchange for a reservation along the Minnesota River and promised annuities. The annuities were consistently withheld, corrupt, or insufficient. The reservation system confined Dakota people to a narrow strip of land far from key sacred sites. By 1862, starvation conditions in the Dakota community were severe, and when a trader (Andrew Myrick) reportedly said "Let them eat grass," he expressed a contempt that catalyzed the U.S.-Dakota War. Land loss was never just economic — it was a severing of the Dakota people from their makóčhe.

The Moon-Based Calendar

Traditional Dakota time is organized around a lunar calendar — each moon (month) is named for a natural phenomenon that characterizes it. Learning these moon names is also learning the ecological calendar of the northern Great Plains: when berries ripen, when waterfowl migrate, when the first frost comes. The language encodes environmental knowledge.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
In Dakota, you do not own the land. The land holds you. This is not merely a poetic sentiment — it is encoded in the grammar. Dakota locative constructions use particles that mean "at," "toward," and "from," placing the speaker in relation to the land rather than positioning the land as property under the speaker's control. The language reflects a world in which a person navigates within a living landscape rather than managing land from above.

The Dakota lunar calendar expresses the same philosophy. Each moon is named for what the land is doing — not for a Roman emperor or a mythological figure. Čhaŋwápe-kasná-wi, the "leaf-falling moon," tells you what October is: the time when leaves fall. Waníčoka-wi, the "middle-winter moon," tells you what January is: the depth of cold. The calendar is an ecological document, a record of attentive, centuries-long observation of the northern Plains environment.

When the U.S. government took the Dakota homeland in 1851 and 1862, it took more than territory. It severed the Dakota people from the specific land that their language, ceremony, and identity grew from. The restoration of Dakota land vocabulary is therefore also a restoration of relationship — a claiming back of the specific knowing that lives in place names, moon names, and the word makóčhe itself.

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: Mní Sota Makhóčhe
docs.text:
Break down the Dakota name for Minnesota Morpheme Meaning Mní water Sota cloudy, milky, sky-reflecting Makhóčhe land, homeland

Analysis: Minnesota's Dakota name — Mní Sota Makhóčhe — means approximately "the land of sky-tinted waters" or "the land where the waters reflect the clouds." The name describes the light quality on Minnesota's lakes and rivers: a particular silver-gray reflectivity that the Dakota people recognized as characteristic of this landscape. The state name "Minnesota" is an anglicization of Mní Sota. Notably, the English name erased Makhóčhe (homeland) — turning a description of a people's homeland into merely a geographic descriptor.

docs.text: Particle Meaning Example ekta at, to (location/direction) Bdóte ekta yá. = He/she goes to Bdóte. etáŋhaŋ from Bdóte etáŋhaŋ hí. = He/she comes from Bdóte. kiŋháŋ at the top of, above Pahá kiŋháŋ waúŋ. = I am at the top of the hill. čhatkáta on the left directional tatkáyela on the right directional

docs.title: Key Vocabulary: Seasons
docs.text:
Dakota Pronunciation English Notes wétȟo WEH-thoh spring Time of renewal blokétu bloh-KEH-too summer Growing season ptaŋyétu ptahn-YEH-too fall / autumn Harvest and preparation waníyetu wah-NEE-yeh-too winter waniyetu wowapi = winter count

Grammar: Seasons as Temporal Nouns

Seasons in Dakota function as temporal nouns — they can appear before the main clause to set time context, or after the verb in a predicate position:

  • Blokétu kiŋ čhaŋpá kiŋ yútapi. = In summer, they eat the berries.
  • Waníyetu kiŋ šni. = It is winter. (Lit. "The winter is.")
  • Wétȟo hí kte. = Spring will come.

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: wiyóhiŋyaŋpa (East)
docs.text:
Break down the word for "east" Morpheme Meaning wiyó- sun -hiŋyaŋpa to rise, to come out

Analysis: wiyóhiŋyaŋpa literally means "where the sun rises" — east is defined not as a fixed abstract point on a compass but as the direction of sunrise, the dynamic daily event of the sun's appearance. Similarly, wiyóhpeyata (west) means "where the sun sets." The Dakota cardinal directions are not geometric abstractions; they are descriptions of the sun's movement through the sky, tying direction to the daily experience of living in relationship with the sun.

In winter, the north wind blows. Ptaŋyétu kiŋ pahá kiŋ ğí. In fall, the hill is brown/golden. Makóčhe kiŋ wakan. The homeland is sacred.

AIS 112 Connection: The Ecological Calendar as Knowledge System

The Dakota lunar calendar is an environmental knowledge system, encoding centuries of careful observation about when plants bloom, when animals migrate, when weather patterns shift. Each moon name is also a behavioral cue: Čhaŋwápe-kasná-wi (leaf-falling moon) is not just "October" — it signals that preparations for winter must intensify. Disruption of Dakota people's connection to the land — through removal, reservation confinement, and allotment — also disrupted this ecological calendar, as people could no longer observe the specific landscapes their moon names described.

docs.title: Chapter 6 Quiz — Makóčhe: Land, Seasons & Directions
Part A — Multiple Choice (10 questions, 2 points each)
docs.text:
1. What does makóčhe mean beyond simply 'land'? Answer

b) Homeland — the land as living relationship, identity, and spiritual ground

makóčhe is not merely geographic land. It encompasses homeland, identity, memory, and spiritual practice rooted in specific places. For Dakota people, the land is a relative, not a resource or property.

a) Sacred earth used in ceremony b) Homeland — the land as living relationship, identity, and spiritual ground c) The soil of the Minnesota River valley specifically d) Any land that belongs to a nation

2. What is Bdóte and why is it significant in Dakota cosmology? Answer

c) The confluence of the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers — the Dakota center of the world and a place of creation in oral tradition

Bdóte is where the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers meet (near present-day Fort Snelling). It is the center of the Dakota world in oral tradition — the place of creation. The U.S. government built Fort Snelling on this site, a profound desecration of the Dakota sacred center.

a) The Dakota word for lake b) A sacred hill near the Black Hills c) The confluence of the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers — the Dakota center of the world and a place of creation in oral tradition d) The name for the first reservation granted to the Dakota people

3. Which Dakota word means 'east' — the direction of sunrise? Answer

b) wiyóhiŋyaŋpa

wiyóhiŋyaŋpa = east, literally "where the sun rises" (wiyó- = sun, -hiŋyaŋpa = to rise/come out). Dakota cardinal directions are defined by the sun's movement, not by fixed compass points.

a) wazíyata b) wiyóhiŋyaŋpa c) itókaga d) wiyóhpeyata

4. What does čhaŋwápe-kasná-wi mean and which month does it correspond to? Answer

c) Leaf-falling moon — approximately October

čhaŋwápe = leaf; kasná = to fall/drop; wi = moon/month. The "leaf-falling moon" corresponds to October, when deciduous trees shed their leaves. This moon name is also a behavioral cue to intensify winter preparations.

a) Berry-ripening moon — approximately August b) Snowblind moon — approximately March c) Leaf-falling moon — approximately October d) Deer-rutting moon — approximately November

5. The word for 'north' in Dakota is: Answer

a) wazíyata

wazíyata = north. It is associated with the white color, cold, and purification in Dakota ceremonial tradition. itókaga = south, wiyóhiŋyaŋpa = east, wiyóhpeyata = west.

a) wazíyata b) itókaga c) wiyóhpeyata d) wiyóhiŋyaŋpa

6. Which treaties stripped the Dakota people of most of their Minnesota homeland in 1851? Answer

b) The Treaties of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota

The 1851 Treaties of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota were signed under pressure and in some cases fraud, ceding nearly all of Dakota's Minnesota territory in exchange for a reservation along the Minnesota River and promised — but often withheld — annuities.

a) The Treaty of Paris and the Northwest Ordinance b) The Treaties of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota c) The Treaty of Laramie and the Homestead Act d) The Treaty of Prairie du Chien and the Land Ordinance

7. What does the word blokétu mean? Answer

c) Summer

blokétu = summer, the growing season. The four seasons are: wétȟo (spring), blokétu (summer), ptaŋyétu (fall), waníyetu (winter).

a) Spring b) Fall c) Summer d) Winter

8. The Dakota locative particle ekta means: Answer

b) At / to (direction or location)

ekta is the locative particle meaning "at" or "to" — it marks the destination or location. Bdóte ekta yá = He/she goes to Bdóte. The contrasting particle is etáŋhaŋ (from).

a) From b) At / to (direction or location) c) Through / across d) Near / beside

9. The name Mní Sota Makhóčhe (Minnesota) is best translated as: Answer

c) Land of sky-tinted/cloudy waters

Mní = water, Sota = cloudy/sky-reflecting, Makhóčhe = homeland/land. The name describes the light quality of Minnesota's lakes. The English state name "Minnesota" dropped the word Makhóčhe (homeland), converting a people's homeland name into a geographic description.

a) Land of the north wind b) Where the rivers meet c) Land of sky-tinted/cloudy waters d) Homeland of the seven fires

10. According to the AIS 112 content, how did Dakota land loss disrupt the lunar calendar knowledge system? Answer

b) Removal and reservation confinement meant Dakota people could no longer observe the specific landscapes their moon names described, severing the calendar from its ecological referents

The lunar calendar names — čhaŋwápe-kasná-wi, Waníčoka-wi, etc. — are descriptions of specific ecological phenomena observable in the northern Great Plains. When Dakota people were confined to reservations and later allotted to individual plots, they lost access to the broader landscape their moon names described.

a) The U.S. government replaced the Dakota calendar with the Gregorian calendar by law b) Removal and reservation confinement meant Dakota people could no longer observe the specific landscapes their moon names described, severing the calendar from its ecological referents c) Missionaries renamed the moons with Christian holidays d) The lunar calendar was preserved without disruption on the reservations

docs.title: Part B — Fill in the Blank (3 questions, 5 points each)
docs.text:
11. The four Dakota seasons in order from spring to winter are: _, _, _, _. Answer
  1. wétȟo (spring)
  2. blokétu (summer)
  3. ptaŋyétu (fall/autumn)
  4. waníyetu (winter)

Memory tip: wétȟo starts with "w" like "waking up" (spring renewal); blokétu has an "b" like "bloom"; ptaŋyétu has "pt" like "plant-harvest"; waníyetu contains waniyetu wowapi (winter count).

12. Translate into Dakota: 'The wind comes from the north.' ____ etáŋhaŋ tȟaté kiŋ hí. Answer

Wazíyata

Wazíyata etáŋhaŋ tȟaté kiŋ hí. — The wind comes from the north. wazíyata = north; etáŋhaŋ = from; tȟaté = wind; kiŋ = the; hí = comes/arrives.

13. The ceremonial color associated with the east (wiyóhiŋyaŋpa) is _, and the color associated with the west (wiyóhpeyata) is _. Answer
  • East: red (šá)
  • West: black (sápa)

The four directional colors: east/red (new beginnings, sunrise), west/black (transformation, sunset), north/white (purification, cold), south/yellow-gold (warmth, growth). These associations appear in ceremony, regalia, and the inípi (sweat lodge).

docs.title: Part C — Short Answer (3 questions, 10 points each)
docs.text:
14. Explain the concept of makóčhe as the Dakota people understood it, and describe how the U.S. seizure of the Dakota homeland — specifically the site of Bdóte — was an ontological violation as well as a political one. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately explains makóčhe as homeland (not mere property), describes Bdóte as the Dakota center of creation, and articulates why building Fort Snelling there was an assault on Dakota being — not just territorial dispossession.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student explains makóčhe correctly but treats the Fort Snelling violation as only political, not ontological.

Sample answer: "Makóčhe is not land as property or geography — it is homeland as living relationship. For Dakota people, the land holds memory, ceremony, and identity. Specific places are relatives — inhabited by spirits, anchored in origin stories, inseparable from who the Dakota people are. Bdóte — the confluence of the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers — was the center of the Dakota world in oral tradition: the place where the Dakota people came into being. When the U.S. government seized this site and built Fort Snelling on it, they did not merely take territory. They built a military installation on the Dakota people's place of creation — a violation not just of political sovereignty but of ontological reality. The Dakota people did not simply lose land; they were severed from the center of their existence."

15. How does the structure of Dakota cardinal direction words (wiyóhiŋyaŋpa = east, wiyóhpeyata = west) reveal a fundamentally different way of organizing space compared to English compass directions? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately analyzes the morphemes (wiyó- = sun, -hiŋyaŋpa = to rise, -hpeyata = to set), explains that Dakota directions are defined by dynamic solar events rather than fixed geometric points, and reflects on what this reveals about a relational, experiential way of knowing space.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student identifies the morphemes correctly but does not reflect on the philosophical difference.

Sample answer: "English compass directions — north, south, east, west — are abstract geometric points derived from magnetic poles. They are fixed, universal, and body-independent. Dakota directions are different: wiyóhiŋyaŋpa (east) means 'where the sun rises,' and wiyóhpeyata (west) means 'where the sun sets.' The root wiyó- means sun; -hiŋyaŋpa means to rise/emerge; -hpeyata means to set/descend. These directions are defined by a dynamic, daily, experiential event — the movement of the sun as observed by a person standing on the land. Space in Dakota is not an abstract grid; it is a relational field organized by the observer's experience of the sun moving overhead. This is consistent with the broader Dakota worldview in which knowledge comes from attentive, embodied observation of the living world."

16. Describe how the 1851 Treaties of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota contributed to the conditions that led to the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862. What role did the withheld annuities and Andrew Myrick's statement play? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately describes the 1851 treaties (land cession, reservation confinement, promised annuities), explains that annuities were withheld or insufficient, describes the starvation conditions by 1862, and references Andrew Myrick's "let them eat grass" statement as a catalyzing moment of contempt. Student may connect land loss to the disruption of makóčhe as discussed in the chapter.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student describes the treaties and withheld annuities but does not connect to the broader land/sovereignty framework, or does not reference Myrick.

Sample answer: "The 1851 Treaties of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota, signed under pressure and in some cases fraudulent conditions, ceded nearly all Dakota land in Minnesota in exchange for a narrow reservation along the Minnesota River and annual annuity payments. The annuities were supposed to compensate for the loss of the vast makóčhe the Dakota people had depended on for food, ceremony, and identity. But the annuities were routinely withheld by corrupt agents, delayed, or insufficient. By 1862, Dakota people on the reservation were facing starvation. When leaders asked trader Andrew Myrick to extend food credit, he reportedly said: 'Let them eat grass' — or their own dung, in some accounts. This statement crystallized the contempt with which the Dakota people were being treated and became a symbol of the structural violence they faced. The war that followed in August 1862 was not an unprovoked attack; it was a desperate response to a decade of broken promises, land loss, and deliberate starvation."

docs.title: Chapter 7 — Wóoyake: Story, Ceremony & Oral Tradition
Summary
docs.text: Chapter 7 introduces the vocabulary and grammar of Dakota storytelling, oral tradition, and ceremony. Students learn about Iktómi — the trickster spider figure — and practice the narrative verb forms and discourse markers used in oral storytelling. AIS 112 content covers the role of oral tradition in Dakota knowledge preservation, the suppression of storytelling in boarding schools, and the ongoing work of language and story revitalization.

docs.title: AIS 112 Cultural Context — Weeks 13–15
docs.text:
Wóoyake — The Living Story

Wóoyake means "story" or "oral narrative," but in Dakota tradition, a story is never merely entertainment. Every traditional story (wóoyake) carries teaching (wóuŋsipi), spiritual content, and community memory. Stories are not read from books — they are spoken, with specific protocols: certain stories may only be told in winter (when snakes and insects are underground and cannot hear), certain stories belong to specific families or keepers, and storytelling requires the audience to participate actively through verbal acknowledgment.

The trickster Iktómi (Spider) is one of the most important figures in Dakota oral tradition. Unlike simple morality tales, Iktómi stories are complex: the trickster is simultaneously foolish and wise, dangerous and creative. Iktómi breaks rules and in doing so reveals what the rules are for. He is the figure who teaches through failure — his own and ours.

Boarding Schools and the Suppression of Story

One of the most systematic cultural losses in the boarding school era was the suppression of oral tradition. When children were separated from their grandparents — the primary keepers of story in Dakota culture — the chain of transmission was broken. Stories that required winter telling, specific family permission, or elder knowledge simply could not be transmitted in an institutional environment where children were forbidden to speak Dakota. Many stories were lost permanently. The revitalization of oral tradition is therefore inseparable from language revitalization — you cannot tell the stories without the language.

Winter Telling Protocols

In traditional Dakota culture, certain stories — especially those involving Iktómi and other spirit beings — may only be told during the winter months, after the first frost and before the last. This protocol is not merely ceremonial. It reflects an ecological and spiritual logic: the creatures who might be disturbed or angered by hearing certain stories are dormant in winter. These protocols survived the boarding school era in many families and communities and are being actively maintained today.

docs.text: Chapter 6 — Makóčhe. Students should have a strong foundation in verb conjugation, seasonal vocabulary, and the wakan concept. Chapter 5's ceremony vocabulary is essential.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Dakota word wóoyake — story — shares a root with oháŋka (to tell, to narrate). In Dakota, telling a story is an action, not a transmission. The teller does not simply relay information; they perform a living relationship between the community, the ancestors, and the world as it exists right now. This is why stories required specific times, specific permissions, and specific audiences.

Iktómi — the Spider Trickster — is one of Dakota oral tradition's most enduring teachers. He is brilliant and stupid. He outwits others and then outwits himself. He breaks every rule and in doing so demonstrates, vividly, why the rules exist. A story about Iktómi is never a simple lesson with a moral at the end; it is an invitation to sit with complexity — to see yourself in the foolish, cunning spider and laugh at yourself without shame.

The grammar of storytelling in Dakota has its own patterns. Discourse markers like héčhel (and so / then it happened) and čha (and then) do the work that "once upon a time" and "and they lived happily ever after" do in English — they signal that a narrative is in progress and mark its transitions. Learning to recognize and use these markers is learning to think in story.

docs.text: Dakota Pronunciation English Notes wóoyake woh-OH-yah-keh story, oral narrative oháŋka oh-HAHN-kah to tell, to narrate Iktómi ik-TOH-mee Spider Trickster The great teacher through failure oháŋ oh-HAHN once / it is said / they say Story-opening marker héčhel HEH-chel and so / then it happened Narrative connector heháŋ heh-HAHN then / at that time Sequential marker čha CHAH and then / so Simple sequence tká TKAH but / however Contrast marker eháŋni eh-HAHN-nee long ago / in the old days Opening temporal marker eyápi eh-YAH-pee they say / it is said Evidential marker — reported speech

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: wóoyake
docs.text:
Break down the word for "story" Morpheme Meaning wó- nominalizing prefix (creates a noun from a verb) -oyake to tell/narrate (related to oháŋka)

Analysis: wóoyake is a nominalization of the verb "to tell" — the story is literally "the telling." In Dakota, story is not a static object (a text, a document) but an action nominalized — frozen in noun form but carrying the energy of telling within it. This grammatical structure encodes the oral tradition's understanding: a story does not exist apart from the telling. Every telling is a new story, shaped by its teller, its audience, and its time.

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: Iktómi
docs.text:
The name and nature of the Spider Trickster Element Meaning Iktómi Spider; the trickster figure

Analysis: The name Iktómi comes from the word for spider (iktómi = spider in some dialects). The spider is an apt trickster: it creates elaborate webs (deceits, schemes, traps) and sometimes catches itself. Iktómi in Dakota oral tradition is not a devil or a pure evil — he is a complex figure who models human behavior at its worst and most creative simultaneously. His stories are told with laughter. The audience is meant to recognize themselves. This is story as mirror, not as lesson.

docs.title: Section 2 — Narrative Grammar
docs.text:
Grammar: Discourse Markers in Storytelling

Dakota narrative uses specific discourse markers to signal story structure. Unlike English, Dakota does not use tense suffixes to mark "past" in narrative — the discourse markers and context do this work:

Marker Use Example oháŋ or eháŋni Opens the story ("Once...") Eháŋni Iktómi... = Long ago, Iktómi... héčhel Signals a consequence ("And so...") Héčhel yá. = And so he went. heháŋ Sequential ("Then...") Heháŋ wičhášta kiŋ hí. = Then the man came. čha Simple sequence ("And then...") Yúta čha yá. = He ate and then went. tká Contrast ("But...") Yá kte tká hí šni. = He was going to go but he didn't come. eyápi Evidential — "they say" Iktómi ohítika eyápi. = Iktómi was brave, they say.

docs.title: Reported Speech and the Evidential eyápi
docs.text:
In oral tradition, it is important to signal that a statement comes from tradition rather than personal witness. The word eyápi (they say / it is said) functions as an evidential marker — it acknowledges that the speaker received this knowledge from others:

Dakota English Eháŋni Iktómi tȟáŋka eyápi. Long ago, Iktómi was great, they say. Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka wóuŋsipi kȟú eyápi. The Great Mystery gave wisdom, they say. Waníyetu wóoyake yápi eyápi. They tell stories in winter, they say.

docs.title: Section 3 — An Iktómi Story Fragment
docs.text:
The following is a simplified teaching narrative in Dakota with interlinear translation. Practice reading it aloud, noting the discourse markers:

Eháŋni Iktómi waŋží tȟáŋka. Long ago, Iktómi was great (important to himself).

Héčhel wakpá ekta yá. And so he went to the river.

Čhokáya šúŋka waŋží wanyáka. In the middle, he saw a dog.

"Mičháŋpá kiŋ lúzahaŋ," eyá. "My horse is fast," he said.

Tká čhaŋpá yuká šni. But he had no horse.

Heháŋ Iktómi įštíŋma. Then Iktómi fell asleep.

Šúŋka kiŋ čhaŋpá kiŋ kiglú. The dog took the horse.

Iktómi kičhí kísapa. Iktómi was fooled.

Oháŋ. (So it is / such is the story.)

Grammar: Story-Closing with Oháŋ

The word oháŋ can open a story (it is said / once) and can also close it — a simple affirmation that the story is complete. This dual use mirrors the circular structure of many Dakota narratives, which end where they begin, or end with a return to the present moment after the narrative journey.

docs.text:
Dakota Pronunciation English Notes wóyuspapi woh-YOOS-pah-pee they gather For ceremony or council yuhápi yoo-HAH-pee they hold / they have Used for ceremony holding wóčhekiye oháŋkapi woh-CHEH-kee-yeh oh-HAHN-kah-pee they offer prayers waŋwíčhayakapi wahn-WEE-chah-yah-kah-pee they watch them / they witness čhantéčhilapi chahn-TEH-chee-lah-pee they love (plural) Closing blessing in ceremony

AIS 112 Connection: Oral Tradition as Knowledge Sovereignty

In contemporary Dakota communities, the revitalization of oral tradition is understood as an act of knowledge sovereignty — the assertion that Dakota knowledge systems are valid, complete, and do not require validation from outside. When Dakota elders tell stories to children in the language, they are not merely preserving a cultural artifact; they are transmitting a complete epistemology — a way of knowing the world. This is why language programs and storytelling initiatives are often connected: without the language, the stories change; without the stories, the language loses its fullest meanings.

docs.text:
Exercise 1: Discourse Markers

Insert the correct discourse marker (oháŋ/eháŋni, héčhel, heháŋ, čha, tká) into these narrative sentences:

  1. Long ago, a woman lived by the river: ____ wiŋyaŋ waŋží wakpá ekta ti.
  2. She ate the berries and then went home: Wóyute kiŋ wayúta ____ tipi ekta yá.
  3. He was going to go but he didn't arrive: Yá kte ____ hí šni.
  4. And so the story happened: ____ wóoyake kiŋ čhéya.

Exercise 2: Translate the Iktómi Fragment

Re-read the Iktómi story fragment in Section 3. Now: a) Identify every discourse marker used and label its function (opening, sequential, contrast, etc.) b) Find the sentence where Iktómi lies. What does this reveal about his character? c) What is the moral lesson implied by the end of the story?

Exercise 3: Create a Short Narrative

Using the storytelling vocabulary and grammar from this chapter, write a 5–7 sentence Dakota narrative (it can be very simple). Your narrative must include: - An opening marker (eháŋni or oháŋ) - At least two sequential discourse markers (héčhel, heháŋ, or čha) - The evidential eyápi at least once - A subject, an action, and a consequence

Chapter 7 Quiz

docs.title: Chapter 7 Quiz — Wóoyake: Story, Ceremony & Oral Tradition
Part A — Multiple Choice (10 questions, 2 points each)
docs.text:
1. What does wóoyake mean, and what does its grammatical structure reveal about Dakota storytelling? Answer

b) Story/oral narrative — a nominalized verb meaning "the telling," revealing that story exists only in the act of narration

wóoyake = wó- (nominalizer) + -oyake (to tell/narrate). Story in Dakota is not a static text but a nominalized action — "the telling." This grammatical structure encodes the oral tradition's understanding that a story only lives in its performance.

a) Story — a noun referring to a written record of past events b) Story/oral narrative — a nominalized verb meaning "the telling," revealing that story exists only in the act of narration c) Prayer — a sacred chant passed between generations d) Memory — the act of remembering ancestors

2. Who is Iktómi in Dakota oral tradition? Answer

c) The Spider Trickster — a complex figure who teaches through failure and self-deception

Iktómi (spider/trickster) is simultaneously foolish and clever, dangerous and creative. His stories are told with laughter because the audience is meant to see themselves in him. He breaks rules and thereby reveals why the rules exist.

a) A great warrior who defeated the U.S. Army b) A sacred spider who created the first humans c) The Spider Trickster — a complex figure who teaches through failure and self-deception d) A benevolent elder spirit who brings good harvests

3. What is the function of the discourse marker eyápi in Dakota storytelling? Answer

b) An evidential marker meaning "they say / it is said" — signaling that the knowledge comes from tradition, not personal witness

eyápi (from eyá = to say, -pi = plural) signals that the speaker received this knowledge from others — from tradition, elders, or oral transmission. This is an important epistemic marker that acknowledges the chain of transmission.

a) A closing marker that ends the story b) An evidential marker meaning "they say / it is said" — signaling that the knowledge comes from tradition, not personal witness c) A time marker meaning "long ago" d) A contrast marker meaning "but"

4. Which discourse marker opens a narrative and can also close it in Dakota storytelling? Answer

a) oháŋ

oháŋ functions both as a story-opening marker ("once / it is said") and as a story-closing affirmation ("so it is / such is the story"). This dual use mirrors the circular structure of many Dakota narratives.

a) oháŋ b) héčhel c) heháŋ d) eháŋni

5. According to the winter telling protocols, why may certain stories only be told during winter months? Answer

c) The creatures who might be disturbed or angered by hearing certain stories are dormant in winter

The winter telling protocol is not arbitrary. It reflects an ecological and spiritual logic: specific stories involving Iktómi and spirit beings cannot be safely told when insects, snakes, and other creatures are awake and might overhear. This protocol survived the boarding school era in many families.

a) Winter nights are longer, giving more time for storytelling b) The stories are about winter events and are contextually appropriate c) The creatures who might be disturbed or angered by hearing certain stories are dormant in winter d) Elders are most available in winter when there is less subsistence work

6. In the Iktómi story fragment, what grammatical role does tká play in the sentence Yá kte tká hí šni? Answer

b) Contrast marker — "but"

tká marks a contrast between what was expected or intended and what actually happened. Yá kte tká hí šni = "He was going to go but he didn't arrive/come." This is the contrast discourse marker, equivalent to English "but" or "however."

a) Sequential marker — "and then" b) Contrast marker — "but" c) Evidential marker — "they say" d) Opening marker — "once"

7. What did the boarding school system do to Dakota oral tradition? Answer

b) By separating children from grandparents (the primary story-keepers) and forbidding Dakota, it broke the chain of transmission, permanently losing many stories

Grandparents were the primary keepers of story in Dakota culture. The boarding school system physically removed children from this relationship and forbidden them to speak Dakota — making it impossible to receive stories that required specific time, permission, and language.

a) It documented oral tradition in written form, preserving it b) By separating children from grandparents (the primary story-keepers) and forbidding Dakota, it broke the chain of transmission, permanently losing many stories c) It allowed oral tradition to continue in a modified English form d) It had little impact because stories were also preserved in pictographic form

8. The discourse marker héčhel signals: Answer

c) A consequence — "and so / so it happened"

héčhel marks a logical or narrative consequence: because X, héčhel Y. "And so he went." "And so it happened." It is different from heháŋ (simple sequential "then") in that it implies cause-effect or narrative momentum.

a) Opening of the story b) Simple sequence — "and then" c) A consequence — "and so / so it happened" d) Reported speech — "they say"

9. The word oháŋka means: Answer

b) To tell a story / to narrate

oháŋka is the verb "to tell, to narrate." The noun form wóoyake is derived from this root with the nominalizing prefix wó-. oháŋka and wóoyake are related as "to tell" is related to "the telling."

a) To remember b) To tell a story / to narrate c) To pray d) To gather for ceremony

10. Why is the revitalization of oral tradition described as an act of 'knowledge sovereignty' in the AIS 112 content? Answer

b) Because oral tradition carries a complete epistemology — a way of knowing the world — that does not require external validation, and its revitalization asserts the validity and completeness of Dakota knowledge systems

Knowledge sovereignty means asserting that one's own knowledge systems are valid and complete without needing Western institutional validation. Dakota oral tradition is not merely cultural heritage — it is a full epistemology: it encodes ecology, ethics, cosmology, and relational knowledge.

a) Because oral tradition was protected under the Treaty of Traverse des Sioux b) Because oral tradition carries a complete epistemology — a way of knowing the world — that does not require external validation, and its revitalization asserts the validity and completeness of Dakota knowledge systems c) Because the U.S. government officially acknowledged oral tradition as a legal form of history d) Because storytelling generates revenue for tribal language programs

docs.title: Part B — Fill in the Blank (3 questions, 5 points each)
docs.text:
11. Complete this story opening in Dakota: ____ Iktómi tȟáŋka eyápi. (Long ago, Iktómi was great, they say.) Answer

Eháŋni

Eháŋni Iktómi tȟáŋka eyápi. — eháŋni = long ago / in the old days. It is the narrative temporal opener, equivalent to "once upon a time." Note also eyápi at the end, the evidential "they say."

12. The discourse marker that signals simple narrative sequence — 'and then' — is ____. Answer

čha (also acceptable: heháŋ)

čha is the simple connective "and then" linking two sequential events: Yúta čha yá = "He ate and then went." heháŋ is slightly stronger, marking a more explicit temporal sequence: "Then, at that point..."

13. In Dakota oral tradition, the chain of story transmission was most directly broken when ____ were separated from their grandparents in boarding schools. Answer

Children (Dakota children / Dakota youth)

Grandparents were the primary keepers of story in Dakota culture. The physical removal of children to distant boarding schools, combined with prohibition on speaking Dakota, severed this intergenerational transmission. Many stories that required elder knowledge, family permission, or winter-telling conditions could not survive this separation.

docs.title: Part C — Short Answer (3 questions, 10 points each)
docs.text:
14. Analyze the Iktómi story fragment from Chapter 7. What does Iktómi do wrong, what are the consequences, and what does this reveal about how Dakota oral tradition uses the trickster figure as a teaching tool? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student identifies Iktómi's boast (claiming to have a fast horse when he has none), the consequence (the dog takes the [imaginary] horse, Iktómi is fooled), and reflects substantively on what the trickster figure achieves — teaching through failure, using humor, and inviting self-recognition rather than moralizing.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student identifies the action and consequence but does not reflect on the teaching function of the trickster.

Sample answer: "In the Iktómi fragment, Iktómi boasts to a dog that his horse is fast — but he has no horse (tká čhaŋpá yuká šni = but he had no horse). He then falls asleep, and the dog takes the (nonexistent) horse. Iktómi is made a fool. The lesson is not delivered through a moral at the end — there is no narrator saying 'and so children, do not lie.' Instead, the story simply ends: Iktómi was fooled. The audience is left to laugh and to recognize themselves. This is the trickster's teaching method: not instruction but mirror. Iktómi's boast is recognizably human — we all inflate ourselves. His failure is also recognizably human. The story works because the audience laughs at Iktómi and, in doing so, laughs at themselves without shame."

15. Explain the function of narrative discourse markers in Dakota storytelling. How do eháŋni, héčhel, heháŋ, čha, and tká work together to structure a narrative, and how do they differ from English narrative conventions? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately explains all five markers with their specific functions (opening, consequence, sequential, simple connective, contrast) and reflects on how Dakota discourse structure differs from English (no past-tense verb forms for narrative past; context and markers carry time information).

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student explains three or more markers correctly but does not compare to English conventions.

Sample answer: "Dakota storytelling uses a set of discourse markers to structure narrative time and logic without relying on verb tense. Eháŋni opens the story in the past ('long ago'); héčhel marks a consequence ('and so it happened'); heháŋ marks simple temporal sequence ('then'); čha is a simple connective ('and then'); and tká marks contrast ('but'). Together, they give a narrative its shape — opening, sequence, surprise, and contrast — using particles rather than verb inflections. In English, narrative past is carried largely by past-tense verb forms ('he went,' 'she said'). In Dakota, the verb forms do not change for narrative past; the markers do the work. This means a Dakota listener attends to discourse-level structure — the markers — to understand narrative time, rather than word-level verb morphology."

16. What does it mean for oral tradition to function as 'knowledge sovereignty,' and why is the revitalization of Dakota storytelling inseparable from language revitalization? Use at least two specific examples from the chapter. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately explains knowledge sovereignty (assertion that indigenous knowledge systems are complete and valid without external validation), explains why language is the carrier of the epistemology (specific vocabulary, evidential markers, discourse structure), and gives at least two specific examples from Chapter 7 (e.g., the evidential eyápi, the winter-telling protocols, the Iktómi stories' teaching method).

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Good explanation of knowledge sovereignty but weak connection to specific chapter examples.

Sample answer: "Knowledge sovereignty means asserting that a community's knowledge systems are internally complete and do not require validation from outside institutions to be legitimate. For Dakota communities, oral tradition is not 'folk history' waiting to be validated by academic historians — it is a full epistemology encoding ecology (čhaŋwápe-kasná-wi = leaf-falling moon, telling you what time of year to prepare for winter), ethics (Iktómi stories teaching through failure and self-recognition), and relational knowledge (the evidential eyápi acknowledging the chain of transmission). This knowledge system lives in the language. The evidential marker eyápi — 'they say' — is not translatable as a simple word; it encodes an entire epistemological stance about how knowledge is received and transmitted. Without the Dakota language, eyápi becomes meaningless. The winter-telling protocols, similarly, cannot be adequately expressed in English — the logic of who can hear which stories, and when, is embedded in a worldview that requires the language to carry it. Revitalizing the language is therefore revitalizing the knowledge sovereignty itself."

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Chapter 8 introduces the vocabulary of Dakota nationhood, political identity, and sovereignty. Students learn the terminology for the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ (Seven Council Fires), treaty history, contemporary Dakota communities, and the language of political self-determination. AIS 112 content provides a comprehensive treatment of the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, the mass execution of 38 Dakota men in Mankato, the Fort Snelling internment camp, and the ongoing work of Dakota sovereignty today.

docs.title: AIS 112 Cultural Context — Weeks 15–16 (Final Unit)
docs.text:
Očhéthi Šakówiŋ — The Seven Council Fires

The Očhéthi Šakówiŋ (often written Oceti Sakowin) — the Seven Council Fires — is the traditional political and cultural confederation of the Dakota, Nakota, and Lakota peoples. The name Očhéthi Šakówiŋ means "Seven (Council) Fires" (očhéthi = fireplace/hearth, šakówiŋ = seven). Each fire represents one of the seven council groups:

  1. Bdewákanthuŋwaŋ (Mdewakanton) — People of the Spirit Lake
  2. Wahpékute — Shooters Among the Leaves
  3. Sisíthuŋwaŋ (Sisseton) — People of the Swampy Land
  4. Wahpéthuŋwaŋ (Wahpeton) — People of the Leaf Village
  5. Iháŋkthuŋwaŋ (Yankton) — People of the End Village
  6. Iháŋkthuŋwaŋna (Yanktonai) — Little People of the End Village
  7. Thítȟuŋwaŋ (Teton/Lakota) — People of the Prairie

The Dakota people are primarily the four eastern fires (1–4). All seven share the Lakȟótiyapi / Dakhótiyapi language family.

The U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 and Its Aftermath

The U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 — called Čhaŋtéšiča (heartbreak/sorrow) in Dakota — was the deadliest conflict on Minnesota soil. It followed a decade of treaty violations, withheld annuity payments, and starvation on the reservation. In August 1862, Dakota warriors led by Little Crow (Tȟašúŋke Čhokípa — His Horse Is Feared) attacked U.S. settlements along the Minnesota River.

After the war, the U.S. government's response was catastrophic: - Military tribunal: 303 Dakota men were sentenced to death in trials lasting as little as five minutes. - Lincoln's review: President Lincoln commuted most sentences, leaving 38 men condemned. - December 26, 1862: The 38 Dakota men were hanged simultaneously in Mankato, Minnesota — the largest mass execution in U.S. history. - Fort Snelling internment: Approximately 1,700 Dakota women, children, and elderly were imprisoned in a concentration camp below Fort Snelling during the winter of 1862–63. Dozens died of disease and exposure. - Exile and bounty: The Dakota people were expelled from Minnesota; the state placed a bounty on Dakota scalps. Survivors were exiled to Crow Creek Reservation in South Dakota, where hundreds more died.

The 38 + 2: Ongoing Commemoration

Every December, the Dakota community commemorates the Mankato executions with the Wokiksuye (remembrance/memorial) ride — a 330-mile horseback ride from Lower Brule, South Dakota to Mankato, Minnesota. This ride has taken place annually since 1987. The "38 + 2" designation refers to the 38 men hanged and two others who were executed later. The commemoration is not merely historical — it is an act of living memory and political witness.

Contemporary Dakota Communities

Dakota people live today in numerous communities across Minnesota, South Dakota, Nebraska, North Dakota, Canada (Manitoba and Saskatchewan), and beyond. In Minnesota, the four Mdewakanton communities — Prairie Island, Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community, Upper Sioux Community, and Lower Sioux Community — have worked for generations on language revitalization, economic development, and the recovery of sacred sites including Bdóte.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The word oyáte means nation, people, community. It is the word the Dakota use to speak of themselves as a collective: Dakota oyáte — the Dakota people, the Dakota nation. The word does not mean "tribe" — that term, with its implications of primitiveness and smallness, was imposed from outside. Oyáte is a word of full political weight: it names a sovereign people with their own governance, their own land, their own laws, and their own relationships to the world.

The Dakota oyáte entered the nineteenth century as the inheritors of a vast, living homeland — Mní Sota Makhóčhe — and emerged from it with their homeland taken, their leaders hanged, their women and children imprisoned, and their people scattered across the continent. This is not ancient history. There are Dakota people living today whose great-grandparents survived the Fort Snelling concentration camp, the Crow Creek exile, and the bounty years. The language that this textbook teaches was spoken by those survivors; it was forbidden to their children; it is being reclaimed by their grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

Learning Dakota is not a neutral academic exercise. It is participation in the ongoing story of a people who have refused to disappear.

docs.title: Morpheme Analysis: Očhéthi Šakówiŋ
docs.text:
Break down the name of the Seven Council Fires Morpheme Meaning Očhéthi fireplace, hearth, council fire Šakówiŋ seven

Analysis: The Seven Council Fires are named for the očhéthi — the hearth fire that is both literally and metaphorically the center of a council gathering. In Dakota governance, a council fire is not merely a meeting — it is the living symbol of the community's continuity. Each of the seven fires represents a distinct group with its own territory, dialect, and council, but all share kinship and the obligation of mutual aid. The name Očhéthi Šakówiŋ is both a political designation and a kinship declaration: we are seven fires who share one fire's warmth.

Analysis: wokiksuye — remembrance — is the word used for the annual December ride commemorating the 38 men hanged at Mankato. Contemporary Dakota Language Revitalization

Today, Dakota language revitalization programs operate at all four Minnesota Dakota communities (Prairie Island, Shakopee, Upper Sioux, Lower Sioux) as well as in Sisseton-Wahpeton, Standing Rock, Crow Creek, and among diaspora communities in Canada. Methods range from master-apprentice programs (pairing fluent elders with learners) to immersion schools for children to university courses like this one. Every speaker gained is an assertion of sovereignty. Every child who learns Háu or Haŋ is continuing a chain of transmission that was nearly broken.

docs.title: Chapter 8 Quiz — Oyáte: Nation, Treaties & Sovereignty
Part A — Multiple Choice (10 questions, 2 points each)
docs.text:
1. What does the word oyáte mean in Dakota? Answer

b) Nation, people, community

oyáte carries the full political weight of "nation" or "people." It is not equivalent to "tribe" (a term with diminishing implications imposed from outside) — it names a sovereign people with their own governance, land, and relationships.

a) Tribe b) Nation, people, community c) Leader, chief d) Land, territory

2. What does Očhéthi Šakówiŋ mean literally? Answer

c) Seven Council Fires

Očhéthi = fireplace/hearth/council fire; šakówiŋ = seven. The name refers to the seven council groups of the Dakota, Nakota, and Lakota peoples who form the broader confederation. Each "fire" represents a distinct but related council group.

a) Seven Sacred Nations b) Seven Brothers of the Prairie c) Seven Council Fires d) Seven Winter Counts

3. On December 26, 1862, 38 Dakota men were executed in Mankato. What made this event historically unprecedented? Answer

b) It was the largest mass execution in United States history

The simultaneous hanging of 38 men on December 26, 1862 in Mankato, Minnesota was and remains the largest mass execution in U.S. history. This followed a military tribunal in which 303 men were originally sentenced to death in trials lasting as little as five minutes.

a) It was the first execution of Native people under federal law b) It was the largest mass execution in United States history c) It was ordered by Abraham Lincoln personally without any review d) It took place on Dakota sacred ground at Bdóte

4. Approximately how many Dakota women, children, and elderly were imprisoned in the Fort Snelling internment camp in winter 1862–63? Answer

c) Approximately 1,700

Following the U.S.-Dakota War, approximately 1,700 Dakota women, children, and elderly were imprisoned below Fort Snelling in a concentration camp during the winter of 1862–63. Many died of disease and exposure. The survivors were then exiled to Crow Creek Reservation in South Dakota.

a) Approximately 100 b) Approximately 500 c) Approximately 1,700 d) Approximately 5,000

5. The Dakota word čhaŋtéšiča — used as a name for the 1862 War — means: Answer

b) Heartbreak / sorrow

čhaŋtéšiča = čhaŋté (heart) + šiča (bad/painful) = heartbreak, sorrow. This is the Dakota people's own name for the conflict of 1862 — not the militarized "War" of U.S. historical naming, but the sorrow that followed a decade of broken promises and starvation.

a) Time of fire b) Heartbreak / sorrow c) The great battle d) Year of the hanging

6. What is the Wokiksuye ride, and how often does it occur? Answer

b) An annual 330-mile horseback commemoration of the 38 men hanged in Mankato — held every December since 1987

The Wokiksuye (remembrance) ride travels approximately 330 miles from Lower Brule, South Dakota to Mankato, Minnesota every December, arriving near the anniversary of the December 26, 1862 executions. It has taken place annually since 1987 and is an act of living political witness.

a) A weekly ceremony held at Bdóte b) An annual 330-mile horseback commemoration of the 38 men hanged in Mankato — held every December since 1987 c) A biennial gathering of all Seven Council Fires communities d) A monthly language revitalization program in Minneapolis

7. The Bdewákanthuŋwaŋ (Mdewakanton) people are best described as: Answer

a) People of Spirit Lake — one of the four eastern Dakota council fires

Bdewákanthuŋwaŋ = Bdewákaŋ (Spirit Lake/Mille Lacs) + thuŋwaŋ (people of). They are the People of Spirit Lake, one of the four eastern Dakota fires. The Mdewakanton communities today include Prairie Island, Shakopee, Upper Sioux, and Lower Sioux in Minnesota.

a) People of Spirit Lake — one of the four eastern Dakota council fires b) People of the Prairie — the westernmost Lakota council fire c) People of the Swampy Land — a northern Dakota group d) Shooters Among the Leaves — a southern Dakota group

8. After the 1863 exile, Dakota people were forced to relocate to which reservation, where hundreds more died? Answer

c) Crow Creek Reservation, South Dakota

Survivors of the Fort Snelling internment were exiled to Crow Creek Reservation in South Dakota — an arid, resource-poor location entirely unlike the Minnesota homeland. Hundreds died of disease, starvation, and exposure in the first years at Crow Creek.

a) Pine Ridge Reservation b) Standing Rock Reservation c) Crow Creek Reservation, South Dakota d) White Earth Reservation, Minnesota

9. The Dakota word wóokihi means: Answer

b) Ability, power, sovereignty

wóokihi means the capacity or power to act — sovereignty in the sense of self-governance and self-determination. It is distinct from political sovereignty as a legal concept; it expresses the lived capacity of a people to determine their own path.

a) Prayer, ceremony b) Ability, power, sovereignty c) Story, narrative d) Treaty, agreement

10. According to the chapter, how many of the original 303 condemned men had their sentences commuted before the December 26, 1862 execution? Answer

b) 265 (reducing the count from 303 to 38)

President Lincoln reviewed the 303 military tribunal sentences and commuted all but 38. The review was itself controversial — conducted rapidly under enormous political pressure from Minnesota officials and settlers who wanted all executions carried out. 265 sentences were commuted; 38 men were executed.

a) 200 (leaving 103 condemned) b) 265 (reducing the count from 303 to 38) c) 290 (leaving 13 condemned) d) 300 (leaving 3 condemned)

docs.title: Part B — Fill in the Blank (3 questions, 5 points each)
docs.text:
11. The largest mass execution in U.S. history took place on December 26, _, in _, Minnesota. Answer
  • Year: 1862
  • City: Mankato

38 Dakota men were hanged simultaneously in Mankato, Minnesota on December 26, 1862. This followed a military tribunal in which 303 men were sentenced to death in trials averaging five minutes. President Lincoln commuted all but 38 sentences.

12. The Dakota phrase meaning 'The Dakota language lives' is: Dakota iápi kiŋ ____. Answer

wičhoni

Dakota iápi kiŋ wičhoni. — The Dakota language lives. wičhoni = life, living. This phrase is used in language revitalization contexts as an affirmation of the language's survival and ongoing presence.

13. The Seven Council Fires are collectively known in Dakota as ____. Answer

Očhéthi Šakówiŋ

Očhéthi = council fire/hearth; šakówiŋ = seven. The Očhéthi Šakówiŋ comprises the seven related council groups of the Dakota (šakówiŋ = seven), Nakota, and Lakota peoples. All seven share the Lakȟótiyapi/Dakhótiyapi language family.

docs.title: Part C — Short Answer (3 questions, 10 points each)
docs.text:
14. Describe the sequence of events from the signing of the 1851 treaties through the 1863 exile of Dakota people. What role did the withholding of annuities play in causing the U.S.-Dakota War? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student provides an accurate chronological sequence covering: 1851 treaties (land cession, promised annuities), withheld annuities, starvation conditions by 1862, the war (August 1862), the military tribunal (303 sentenced), Lincoln's commutation (38 remain), Mankato executions (December 26, 1862), Fort Snelling internment (1862–63), and Crow Creek exile (1863). Student clearly explains the role of withheld annuities in creating the starvation conditions that catalyzed the war.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Accurate but incomplete sequence; may miss Crow Creek or Fort Snelling.

Sample answer: "The 1851 Treaties of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota stripped Dakota people of most of their Minnesota homeland in exchange for a narrow reservation along the Minnesota River and annual annuity payments. Almost immediately, these annuities were withheld, delayed, or diverted by corrupt agents. By 1861–62, reservation conditions were desperate — people were starving. When Dakota leaders attempted to access food stores, trader Andrew Myrick reportedly said 'Let them eat grass.' In August 1862, Dakota warriors led by Little Crow attacked U.S. settlements along the Minnesota River, beginning the U.S.-Dakota War. After the Dakota forces surrendered following the Battle of Wood Lake in September, a military tribunal sentenced 303 men to death in trials averaging five minutes each. President Lincoln reviewed the sentences and commuted all but 38. On December 26, 1862 — the largest mass execution in U.S. history — 38 Dakota men were hanged simultaneously in Mankato. That same winter, approximately 1,700 Dakota women, children, and elderly were imprisoned below Fort Snelling, where dozens died of disease and exposure. In 1863, surviving Dakota people were expelled from Minnesota, with a state bounty placed on Dakota scalps, and the survivors were exiled to the desolate Crow Creek Reservation in South Dakota, where hundreds more died."

15. Explain the meaning of wokiksuye — remembrance — and describe the Wokiksuye ride. Why is this act of annual commemoration also an act of political sovereignty? Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student accurately breaks down wokiksuye morphologically (or describes its meaning), describes the annual 330-mile ride from Lower Brule to Mankato, and articulates why annual commemoration is a political act — asserting continuity, refusing erasure, making visible the connection between the living and the 38.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Accurate description of the ride but shallow analysis of its political dimension.

Sample answer: "Wokiksuye breaks down as wo- (nominalizer) + -kik- (reflexive/reciprocal) + -suye (to remember). It is a collective self-remembering — the community remembering itself through its dead. Every December since 1987, riders travel approximately 330 miles from Lower Brule, South Dakota to Mankato, Minnesota, arriving near the anniversary of the December 26, 1862 executions. The ride is an act of political sovereignty because it refuses the erasure that the U.S. government attempted in 1862 and after. To say 'we remember' is to assert that the connection between the living Dakota people and the 38 men is unbroken — that the executions did not end the Dakota nation, that the exile did not sever the people from their history. The ride makes this assertion physically, publicly, and annually. It is not nostalgia; it is witness. And it takes place on the land — on the makóčhe — from which the Dakota people were expelled, demonstrating that the relationship to the land also continues."

16. This is the final chapter of the course. Reflect on the arc of this textbook: from Háu / Haŋ (greetings, Chapter 1) to Oyáte (nation and sovereignty, Chapter 8). How has learning the Dakota language changed or deepened your understanding of Dakota history, culture, and the meaning of language itself? Reference at least three specific concepts or vocabulary items from different chapters in your answer. Rubric / Sample Answer

Full credit (10 pts): Student reflects substantively on personal growth across the course, demonstrates genuine engagement with at least three specific concepts from different chapters, and connects language learning to the broader themes of sovereignty, relationship, and resistance that the course has developed. Reflection shows critical thinking, not just summary.

Partial credit (5–7 pts): Student references course content but reflection is primarily summary rather than synthesis; or fewer than three chapters represented.

Sample answer: "Beginning this course with Háu / Haŋ — two different greetings depending on the speaker's gender — I thought I was learning a vocabulary distinction. By the end, I understand I was encountering a whole philosophy of relationship: that who you are shapes how you speak, and how you speak shapes who you are in relation to others. In Chapter 2, learning that color words are stative verbs — that 'red' is something a thing is in, not something it has — changed how I understood descriptive language itself. In Chapter 5, learning that Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ is a personal declaration of kinship with all living beings taught me that Dakota spirituality is not a religion compartmentalized from life but a grammar of relationship that infuses everything. And in Chapter 8, learning the word wokiksuye — remembrance as collective self-memory, not nostalgia — taught me that language revitalization is not an academic preservation project. It is the active refusal of erasure. Every Dakota word I learn connects me, however distantly, to a chain of transmission that was nearly destroyed and is still being rebuilt. That is not a neutral thing. It is a responsibility."

2. Wačháŋtognaka is the Dakota virtue of:

A) Generosity B) Bravery C) Wisdom D) Truth Answer: A

3. The season waníyetu means:

A) Spring B) Summer C) Fall D) Winter Answer: D

4. Bdóte refers to:

A) The Missouri River B) The confluence of the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers — the Dakota spiritual and geographic center C) The Black Hills D) Lake Superior Answer: B

5. The 1851 Treaty of Traverse des Sioux:

A) Granted Dakota citizenship B) Ceded most of southern and western Minnesota, leaving a narrow strip along the Minnesota River C) Established reservation boundaries that still exist D) Gave Dakota people permanent hunting rights Answer: B

6. What occurred in Mankato, Minnesota on December 26, 1862?

A) The signing of the 1862 peace treaty B) The battle of Mankato C) The mass execution of 38 Dakota men — the largest mass execution in U.S. history D) The establishment of the Dakota reservation Answer: C

7. Iktómi in Dakota oral tradition is:

A) A sacred healing ceremony B) The sun deity C) The spider trickster whose stories carry moral teachings D) A type of ceremonial song Answer: C

8. The phrase for 'east' in Dakota:

A) Wazíyata B) Itókaga C) Wiyóhiŋyaŋpa D) Wiyóhpeyata Answer: C — Wiyóhiŋyaŋpa (where the sun comes from)

9. Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka means:

A) Sacred pipe B) Great Mystery / Great Spirit C) Seven Grandfather Teachings D) All my relations Answer: B

10. The Code of Indian Offenses (1883) is significant because:

A) It established tribal courts B) It criminalized Native ceremonies, dances, and traditional healing practices C) It guaranteed religious freedom D) It returned stolen land Answer: B

11. Wokiksuye means:

A) Treaty B) Sovereignty C) Remembrance / commemoration D) Oral tradition Answer: C (as in the Wokiksuye memorial ride)

12. The direction Wazíyata (north) is associated with:

A) New beginnings and dawn B) Warmth and growth C) The cold winds, wisdom, and rest D) Reflection and endings Answer: C

13. After the 1862 war, Dakota people who were not executed were:

A) Imprisoned at Fort Snelling then exiled to Crow Creek, South Dakota B) Allowed to remain in Minnesota on reduced land C) Relocated to Canada D) Given U.S. citizenship Answer: A

14. The moon čhaŋwápe-kasná-wi refers to:

A) The leaf-falling / harvest moon (October equivalent) B) The planting moon C) The berry moon D) The ice-forming moon Answer: A

15. Which statement best describes contemporary Dakota language revitalization?

A) Dakota is no longer spoken by anyone B) Revitalization is unnecessary because English serves all needs C) Dakota communities actively maintain immersion programs, master-apprentice partnerships, and language nests to pass the language to new generations D) Revitalization is complete — everyone is fluent again Answer: C

docs.title: Part D — Short Writing (15 points)
docs.text:
Prompt: Write 5–7 Dakota sentences describing a season (wétȟo, blokétu, ptaŋyétu, or waníyetu). Include: the season name, at least one moon name for that season, a weather or nature observation, a traditional activity, and a future tense sentence. Provide English translations.

Scoring: 3 pts Dakota accuracy + 3 pts vocabulary range + 3 pts grammar (SOV, -kte) + 3 pts cultural content + 3 pts coherence

docs.title: Part E — Extended Essay (15 points)
docs.text:
Choose ONE prompt. Write 10–15 sentences. Underline at least 8 Dakota words or phrases. Assessed on language accuracy AND historical/cultural depth.

Option A — Language and Worldview: How does the Dakota language encode a different understanding of the world than English? Use examples from at least THREE chapters (e.g., SOV order, stative verbs, passive name construction, makóčhe as homeland, Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ). What surprised you most, and what did it teach you about how language shapes thought?

Option B — The 1862 War and Its Aftermath: Describe the events of 1862–1863 in Dakota history. What were the causes of the U.S.-Dakota War? What happened at Fort Snelling and Mankato? How does the language — particularly wokiksuye (remembrance) and Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ (all my relations) — help us understand how Dakota people carry this history? What is the Wokiksuye memorial ride and why does it matter today?

Option C — Language Revitalization: Why does Dakota language revitalization matter? Connect your answer to vocabulary from at least THREE chapters — including Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ (Ch. 5), oral tradition and Wóoyake (Ch. 7), and Oyáte (Ch. 8). What role does language play in sovereignty, healing, and cultural continuity? What is one thing you will carry from this course?

Covers: Chapters 1–4 | Total: 100 pts | Time: 60 min | ACTFL Target: Novice Low → Mid

Format

docs.title: Part A — Multiple Choice (30 points)
docs.text:
1. Which greeting does a Dakota man use?

A) Háu | B) Haŋ | C) Pidámayaye | D) Háŋ | Answer: A

2. The Dakota word order is:

A) SVO (Subject-Verb-Object) like English B) SOV (Subject-Object-Verb) — verb comes last C) VSO (Verb-Subject-Object) D) Free order with no pattern Answer: B

3. How do you form the future tense in Dakota?

A) Add a prefix wí- before the verb B) Add the suffix -kte after the verb C) Change the vowel of the verb root D) Use a separate auxiliary word Answer: B

4. The color 'red' as a stative verb in Dakota is:

A) šá B) tó C) sápa D) ğí Answer: A — šá

5. 'My name is ___' in Dakota uses the construction:

A) ___ emítiyapi B) ___ emáčiyapi C) ___ etáŋhaŋ waúŋ D) ___ mitiyóšpaye Answer: B

6. Numbers in Dakota greater than ten are formed by:

A) Using separate words for each digit B) Using wikčémna (ten) with a multiplier, then adding units C) Borrowing English number words D) Using a completely separate number system for teens Answer: B e.g., wikčémna núŋpa (twenty) + ákeyaŋ waŋží (plus one) = 21

7. 'I do not eat' in Dakota uses:

A) Hiyá + verb B) The negation suffix -šni on the verb C) A separate word né before the verb D) Reversing the SOV order Answer: B

8. The tiyóšpaye is:

A) A type of food storage B) The extended family band — the basic social unit C) A ceremonial lodge D) The Dakota national council Answer: B

9. Dakota stative verbs for colors:

A) Must always follow the noun they describe B) Function as predicates — 'the dog is-black' not 'the black dog' C) Are identical in all grammatical persons D) Only apply to animate nouns Answer: B

10. 'My heart' in Dakota:

A) čhaŋté mítawa B) mičháŋte C) čhaŋté emáčiyapi D) mitiyóšpaye čhaŋté Answer: B — mičháŋte (possessive prefix mi- + čhaŋté)

11. How do you say 'I am sick / something hurts me' in Dakota?

A) Wičhášta mayázaŋ B) Mayázaŋ (lit. "it pains me") C) Sápa mayázaŋ D) Mičháŋte yá Answer: B — Mayázaŋ

12. The Očhéthi Šakówiŋ consists of how many council fires?

A) 4 | B) 5 | C) 7 | D) 13 | Answer: C

13. 'You're welcome / it's nothing' in Dakota:

A) Pidámayaye B) Tokhéya C) Tókheča šni D) Háŋ Answer: C — Tókheča šni (lit. "it's not different")

14. Pre-contact Dakota leadership was based on:

A) Hereditary chieftainship B) Earned respect through wisdom, bravery, and generosity C) Military conquest D) Religious appointment Answer: B

15. Which word means 'woman' in Dakota?

A) Wíčhaša B) Wiŋyaŋ C) Oyáte D) Akíčhita Answer: B — Wiŋyaŋ

docs.title: Part B — Fill in the Blank (30 points)
docs.text:
1. The Dakota number for "seven": ___
  2. Dakota word order: Subject — ___ — Verb
  3. To negate a Dakota verb, add the suffix ___
  4. The stative verb for "it is black" in Dakota: ___
  5. "Thank you" in Dakota: ___
  6. The extended family band in Dakota society: ___
  7. Future tense suffix in Dakota: ___
  8. "I am from ___" in Dakota: ___ etáŋhaŋ waúŋ
  9. "It hurts / I am sick" in Dakota: ___
  10. The four seasons: Spring _______, Summer _______, Fall _______, Winter _______

  2. Tiyóšpaye | 22. -kte | 23. [place name] | 24. Mayázaŋ
