docs.title: Part C — Translation (20 points)
docs.text:
Translate each sentence into English (4 pts each):

  1. James emáčiyapi. Bdewákhaŋthuŋwaŋ etáŋhaŋ waúŋ.
  2. Šúŋka waŋ sápa yá.
  3. Waŋží, núŋpa, yámni, tópa, záptaŋ.
  4. Mičháŋte mayázaŋ. Pidámayaye.
  5. Wičhášta kiŋ wóuŋsipi-kte.
Part C Answers
  1. My name is James. I am from Mdewakanton.
  2. A dog is black. (There is a black dog.)
  3. One, two, three, four, five.
  4. My heart hurts. Thank you.
  5. The man will work / do daily activities.

docs.title: Part D — Essay (20 points)
docs.text:
Choose ONE prompt. Write 8–12 sentences. Underline at least 5 Dakota words used correctly.

Option A: Explain the tiyóšpaye system and pre-contact Dakota political structure. How does the language reflect Dakota social values (passive name construction, gender speech, etc.)?

Option B: Explain the SOV word order and the stative verb system for colors in Dakota. Give 4 example sentences showing both features, with translations.

Option C: Describe what you would say in a formal Dakota introduction — name, origin, and closing. Explain the cultural significance of each element and how it differs from an English introduction.

docs.title: FOUND — Foundation Concepts
docs.text: Core meta-concepts about the Dakota language: what it is, its orthography system, and how it relates to the broader Siouan language family. These are the zero-dependency concepts that everything else builds on.

docs.title: GREET — Greetings & Identity
docs.text: All greeting phrases, name construction patterns, leave-taking expressions, and affirmation/negation words. These are typically the first concepts introduced in Chapter 1.

docs.title: GRAM — Grammar & Structure
docs.text: Grammatical rules, patterns, and structures: word order (SOV), verb suffixes (-kte, -šni), pronoun system, stative verb structure, possessive prefixes, article use, and narrative connectors.

docs.title: VOCAB — Vocabulary
docs.text: Individual Dakota lexical items introduced across all chapters — body parts, family terms, seasonal words, directional words, ceremonial vocabulary, and narrative language.

docs.title: NUM — Numbers & Counting
docs.text: The Dakota number system from 1 through 1,000, including how numbers above ten are formed, multiples of ten, and the cultural context of Dakota counting.

docs.title: CULT — Culture & Values
docs.text: Cultural concepts, values (wačháŋtognaka, ohítika, ksapá), the relational worldview (Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ), ceremonial traditions, kinship systems, oral tradition pedagogy, and environmental ethics. The largest category reflecting the AIS 112 integration.

docs.title: HIST — History
docs.text: Historical events, political structures, and geographic contexts: pre-contact Dakota society, trade networks, the treaty period (1851, 1858), U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, Fort Snelling, Mankato executions, exile, and contemporary community context.

docs.title: REV — Language Revitalization
docs.text: Concepts related to the ongoing revitalization of Dakota: language endangerment, sovereignty, immersion programs, master-apprentice models, community organizations (Dakhóta Iápi Okhódakičhiye), and ethical dimensions of language learning.

docs.title: LANG — ACTFL & Proficiency
docs.text: The ACTFL proficiency framework as applied to this course: Novice Low, Mid, High, and Intermediate Low descriptors and their chapter alignment.

docs.title: MISC — Miscellaneous
docs.text: Cross-cutting concepts that don't fit neatly into one category, including learner ethics, AI and language ethics, and land acknowledgment practice.

docs.text:
Add the following section to docs/course-description.md before proceeding:

## Learning Outcomes

After completing this course, students will be able to:

### Remember
- Recall the gender-specific greeting forms (Háu / Haŋ) and their appropriate use
- List the numbers 1–1,000 in Dakota
- Name the Seven Council Fires (Očhéthi Šakówiŋ) and their dialect groupings
- Identify the Standard Dakota Orthography characters and accent marks
- Recall the four cardinal directions in Dakota

### Understand
- Explain the Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) word order of Dakota
- Describe how stative verbs function as color/quality descriptors
- Explain the cultural significance of the tiyóšpaye (extended family band)
- Summarize the events of the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 and its aftermath
- Explain the concept of Mitákuye Oyásʼiŋ (All my relations) and its worldview implications

### Apply
- Introduce themselves in Dakota using name, origin, and closing
- Form future tense (-kte) and negation (-šni) on Dakota verbs
- Use Dakota vocabulary to describe seasons, land, and directions
- Apply passive name construction correctly (emáčiyapi vs. eníčiyapi)
- Construct SOV sentences using learned vocabulary

### Analyze
- Compare Dakota SOV grammar to English SVO order
- Distinguish between stative verbs and action verbs in Dakota
- Examine how treaty language affected Dakota land and sovereignty
- Analyze how Dakota vocabulary encodes a relational worldview

### Evaluate
- Assess the significance of language revitalization for Dakota communities
- Evaluate the impact of boarding school policies on Indigenous languages
- Judge the role of oral tradition in preserving cultural knowledge

### Create
- Compose a formal Dakota self-introduction (name, origin, closing)
- Write a short paragraph about a season using Dakota vocabulary
- Design a short dialogue between two speakers using greetings and identity phrases
- Produce a cultural reflection connecting language learning to treaty history

## Topics Excluded

This course does NOT cover:
- Lakota or Nakota dialects (though context is provided)
- Advanced Dakota grammar beyond Novice High level
- Writing systems other than Standard Dakota Orthography
- Ceremonially restricted cultural content
- Speaking fluency beyond basic communicative phrases
